subject: assessor's roll
body:
Good morning and happy Monday!!
A couple of questions on what power a town board or city council has...
Does the board/council have any say over the LOA? I thought that was solely determined by the assessor.
If the board/council wants the assessor (prior to Tentative Roll) to pull the reassessment because they are getting so much backlash from property owners
(and we all know they can't handle the heat), can they force the assessor to go back to the prior year's values? I have seen them put political pressure on the assessor, but I thought that ultimately, it is the assessor's decision whether to pull it, or not.
Any feedback would be greatly appreciated.
Keep cool... Going up to 90 today.
~ Meghan.

Exemption of Church
body:
Good morning,
It just came to our attention that there are delinquent taxes on a church in one of our towns.  This church has never applied for the non profit exemption.  Now they want the county to wipe out the delinquent tax bills.  The assessor told
the church that she won't correct there bill because there is nothing to correct and now the church has come to myself and the CFO here and want's to know if there is something we can do.  I don't recommend that we just wipe these bills out because they admitted
they didn't apply for the exemption they thought they would just be exempt because they are a church.    That would be bad because then every non profit or person that didn't apply for an exemption would expect their bill to be corrected.
I am not sure if my CFO will agree or if he will want to correct the prior years.  Any suggestion on how to handle this would be greatly appreciated.  I believe I read somewhere that NYS doesn't recognize that churches are automatically
exempt and that their failure to apply for an exemption doesn't mean that they are not responsible for taxes that are generated from their failure to apply.
Thank you in advance.
Debbie
Deborah J. McGrath
Director Real Property Tax Services
Rensselaer County
(518)270-2775
dmcgrath@renscony.gov

subject: Battery storage under RPTL 487
body:
Hey all,
I had thought that battery storage had to be in conjunction with a solar or other alternative energy source to get a PILOT under 487, but in re-reading the law, it looks like battery storage connected to the grid is eligible for a PILOT
even without being part of a solar project, because it says "or" below. Am I reading that right?
"Real property that contains a solar energy, wind energy, farm waste energy, micro-hydroelectric energy, fuel cell electric generating, micro-combined heat and power generating equipment, or an electric energy storage system approved by
the State Energy Research and Development Authority is exempt from taxation for a period of 15 years to the extent of any increase in assessed value due to the system. Such property is liable for special ad valorem levies and special assessments. The exemption
as reenacted in 1990 is subject to local option."
https://www.tax.ny.gov/research/property/assess/manuals/vol4/pt1/sec4_01/sec487.htm
We have some battery storage connected to solar projects that are part of PILOTs done before I started here, and we have three battery storage projects that went through our IDA to get IDA PILOTs (still not happy about that, but I have
been able to contain my anger into a slow simmer, so I have that going for me). But we have not had any battery projects asking for 487 PILOTs-- until now.
And what rate are you all doing battery storage? We had done the solar ones at $4,000 per MW of storage, compared to the $10,000 per MW that we get for solar (Central Hudson and Orange & Rockland have some of the highest rates this side
of Hawaii, so it justifies the high PILOT rates. Don't at me, y'all).
Paul Wiley
Director
Orange County Office of Real Property

Goshen, NY 10924

it.
is there anything anywhere that you know of that could compel a Director of Real Property to have to attend a BAR, particularly in regard to investigating the claims of a taxpayer against an assessor?
Short answer:  Yes -- in New York, a
Board of Assessment Review (BAR) can compel certain people to appear, but
there is no statute that compels a County Director of Real Property Tax Services to attend a BAR hearing. The law
does compel the assessor or their staff to attend, and it gives the BAR power to compel
"any person" to appear if relevant to a complaint, but the Director is not explicitly mandated by statute to attend BAR hearings.
Below is the detailed breakdown, with citations and the key legal hooks you can rely on.
What the law
does say about compelling attendance
1. BAR's statutory power to compel witnesses
Under Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) § 525(2), the BAR may:
Administer oaths
Take testimony
Require "any other person" to appear and be examined
Require production of papers relevant to the assessment
This is broad. It means the BAR
can require someone to appear if the testimony is relevant to the complaint.
BUT:  The statute only imposes a
penalty (loss of right to assessment reduction) on the taxpayer who refuses to appear -- not on government officials.
So while the BAR may request or require the Director to appear,
there is no statutory enforcement mechanism if the Director refuses.
2. Who must attend BAR hearings?
RPTL § 523‑a(4) explicitly requires:
"The assessor or a member of his or her staff shall attend all hearings" of administrative hearing panels.
This requirement applies to assessors, not Directors of Real Property Tax Services.
3. What the Director of Real Property Tax Services is required to do
RPTL § 1532 lists the Director's duties. These include:
Advising assessors
Preparing tax maps
Providing advisory appraisals
Assisting acting BARs under § 527
Notably absent:  Any requirement that the Director attend BAR hearings or respond to BAR investigative demands.
The only time the Director is explicitly required to act in relation to BAR proceedings is when:
A BAR fails to meet (§ 527), and
The assessor notifies the Director, who must then organize an acting BAR.
Even here, the Director's role is administrative -- not testimonial.
So can a BAR
force a Director to appear?
Legally:
The BAR has broad authority to "require any person" to appear (§ 525).
But there is no statutory penalty if the Director refuses.
There is no statute explicitly obligating the Director to attend.
Practically:
A BAR can request the Director's appearance.
A BAR can issue a formal demand under § 525.
But the Director can decline without legal consequence.
Could a taxpayer compel the Director to appear?
A taxpayer cannot compel the Director to appear before the BAR.
A taxpayer could potentially subpoena the Director in:
An Article 7 tax certiorari proceeding, or
An Article 78 proceeding alleging failure of duty.
But that is court action, not BAR authority.
Bottom line
There is no law in New York that compels a Director of Real Property Tax Services to attend a BAR hearing, even when the BAR is investigating a taxpayer's claims against
an assessor.
The BAR may request or attempt to require attendance under § 525, but the Director is not legally obligated to comply, and there is no statutory penalty for refusal.

I asked a low budget "trusty AI" your question and below is the response.... "🤣 Take what you want from it.
is there anything anywhere that you know of that could compel a Director of Real Property to have to attend a BAR, particularly in regard to investigating the claims of a taxpayer against an assessor?
Short answer:  Yes -- in New York, a Board of Assessment Review (BAR)
can compel certain people to appear, but there is no statute that compels a County Director of Real Property Tax Services to attend a BAR hearing. The law
does compel the assessor or their staff to attend, and it gives the BAR power to compel
"any person" to appear if relevant to a complaint, but the Director is not explicitly mandated by statute to attend BAR hearings.
Below is the detailed breakdown, with citations and the key legal hooks you can rely on.
📌 What the law does say about compelling attendance
1. BAR's statutory power to compel witnesses
Under Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) § 525(2), the BAR may:
Administer oaths
Take testimony
Require "any other person" to appear and be examined
Require production of papers relevant to the assessment
This is broad. It means the BAR can require someone to appear if the testimony is relevant to the complaint.
BUT:  The statute only imposes a penalty (loss of right to assessment reduction) on the
taxpayer who refuses to appear -- not on government officials.
So while the BAR may request or require the Director to appear, there is no statutory enforcement mechanism if the Director refuses.
2. Who must attend BAR hearings?
RPTL § 523‑a(4) explicitly requires:
"The assessor or a member of his or her staff shall attend all hearings" of administrative hearing panels.
This requirement applies to assessors, not Directors of Real Property Tax Services.
3. What the Director of Real Property Tax Services is required to do
RPTL § 1532 lists the Director's duties. These include:
Advising assessors
Preparing tax maps
Providing advisory appraisals
Assisting acting BARs under § 527
Notably absent:  Any requirement that the Director attend BAR hearings or respond to BAR investigative demands.
The only time the Director is explicitly required to act in relation to BAR proceedings is when:
A BAR fails to meet (§ 527), and
The assessor notifies the Director, who must then organize an acting BAR.
Even here, the Director's role is administrative -- not testimonial.
📌 So can a BAR force a Director to appear?
Legally:
The BAR has broad authority to "require any person" to appear (§ 525).
But there is no statutory penalty if the Director refuses.
There is no statute explicitly obligating the Director to attend.
Practically:
A BAR can request the Director's appearance.
A BAR can issue a formal demand under § 525.
But the Director can decline without legal consequence.
📌 Could a taxpayer compel the Director to appear?
A taxpayer cannot compel the Director to appear before the BAR.
A taxpayer could potentially subpoena the Director in:
An Article 7 tax certiorari proceeding, or
An Article 78 proceeding alleging failure of duty.
But that is court action, not BAR authority.
📌 Bottom line
There is no law in New York that compels a Director of Real Property Tax Services to attend a BAR hearing, even when the BAR is investigating a taxpayer's claims against an assessor.
The BAR may request or attempt to require attendance under § 525, but the Director is not legally obligated to comply, and there is no statutory penalty for refusal.
"

Memorial Day Weekend Greetings Assessor Pastena,

As I write this, I have not had this FOIL acknowledged.
With this FOIL unacknowledged and unfulfilled, and Monday being Memorial Day, and Tuesday being Grievance Day, please know that without further communication I will be required to infer what is inferable from the silence and the past record
a similar FOIL generated upon filament, and this as a pattern. Furthermore, and again this year (but preemptively relative to a RP 524 filing), please be aware that I intend to requesting that the schedule of the Orange County Director of Real Property Tax
Services (cc:'d) be accommodated to include the Officer in a scheduled hearing before our BAR. The cause of this remains an ongoing failure our your Office relative to my request for information, inclusive of what is referenced in law, and this for the purpose
of the due diligence necessary to properly file under RPTL §554(3).
Please be cognizant that the silence,
as a pattern relative to duties and obligations of an Assessor, and
how this is relevant concerning the color of your Office's presumptive, and
particularly the valuation matters that are integral to the locked in property damage due to our abruptly changed climate system, and
this with willful silence, not being dutifully acknowledged, and
this for whatever the cause(s) and/or reason(s),
constitutes ongoing injury regarding which, by statute, provides for the Directory to investigate and report on once I have been provided all the information I have requested, and may additionally need to request, to do so.
In the meantime, does the meaning of what is memorialized this weekend dishonorably languishes on [at least] your watch?
Regardless, and since Eternal Vigilance is the Price of Liberty, and Oaths of Office, relative to one's best ability to be so honorable, constitute a matter of human agency, may we yet march in common cause.

Greg

subject: town attorney won't handle small claims
body:
CAUTION:
Good morning -
In one of my towns, there is an Article 7 that was filed several years ago and has yet to be settled.
The assessor was just contacted by the owner's attorney who was looking for the town attorney's contact info, stating that the town missed a court date. The assessor reached out to the town attorney, who stated
that he does not handle property tax litigation, and the town should have a litigation attorney for this. The assessor asked the town clerk about it, and she said that they have only used one attorney, and suggested that the assessor reach out to me.
Generally, the town attorney takes care of Article 7 cases. Have you ever had a case where they refused to do so? Did the county attorney take over? Did they charge the town back?
Thank you for any input.

type in a parcel ID and after about 10 seconds of waiting it either:
Kicks back to the search screenGoes to the parcel but every action takes several seconds
If it kicks back to the search screen then clicking the back arrow actually loads the parcel you were intending to view. I can replicate this both with a citrix connection via a web browser and connected directly

§   523-a.   Temporary   members   of  boards  of  assessment  review;
administrative hearing panels. 1. The  legislative  body  of  any  local

twenty-three of this title and which served on such  board  for  hearing
complaints  in  the  previous  year.  Such  temporary  members  shall be
appointed to one-year terms of office and shall be subject to  the  same
qualifications,  training  and disclosure requirements as members of the
board of assessment review, as provided in subdivisions one,  one-a  and
two  of  section  five  hundred twenty-three of this title and any other
applicable law; provided, however, such temporary members shall not hear
complaints  unless  such  appointee  has  received  a   certificate   of
attendance  for the required training course within twelve months of the
date on which complaints are to be heard.
3. The chairman of the board of assessment review shall assign  panels
to hear complaints in relation to assessments consisting of at least one
member  appointed  pursuant to section five hundred twenty-three of this
title and no more than two temporary members appointed pursuant to  this
section.   Such panels shall have the same powers and duties as those of
the  board  of  assessment  review  pursuant  to  section  five  hundred
twenty-five of this title except that they shall not determine the final
assessment  of  the  real property of each complainant, but shall make a
recommendation with respect thereto to the board of assessment review.
4. The assessor or a member of his  or  her  staff  shall  attend  all
hearings  of  the administrative hearing panels, shall have the right to
be heard on any complaint and, upon request, shall  have  the  right  to
have  his  or  her remarks with respect to any complaint recorded in the
minutes of the panel.
5. Not later than twenty days prior to the last date provided  by  law
for  the  completion  and  filing  of  the  final  assessment roll, each
administrative hearing panel shall submit a recommendation with  respect
to each complaint heard by it to the chairman of the board of assessment
review.  The  board  of  assessment  review shall forthwith consider the
recommendations of each panel. If a majority of the members of the board
of assessment review disagree with one or more recommendations, it shall
schedule hearings thereon for a day no later than five days prior to the
date set by law for the completion and filing of  the  final  assessment
roll  and  shall notify the assessor and the complainant of the time and
place of the hearings. Following this hearing, the board  of  assessment
review  shall  determine  the  final  assessment  of  the  complainant's
property. In all other cases, the recommendation of  the  administrative
hearing  panel shall be adopted by the board of assessment review as its
determination of the final assessment.
6. The legislative body of the local government or village may adopt a
resolution  providing  that  the  temporary  members  of  the  board  of
assessment  review  appointed pursuant to this section shall be paid for
their respective services. Such resolution, if adopted,  shall  fix  the
amount of such compensation.

subject: Re: BAR Question
body:
CAUTION:
And you can't use the temporary hearing panels as a temporary BAR member.
The hearing panels supplement the full BAR - it doesn't replace them.  In the case of a 3 person BAR, you appoint 6 temporary panel members and you create 3 hearing panels.  Each panel is chaired
by a BAR member and 2 temporary hearing members.  This is typically done in a year of a revaluation so that you can hear more complaints at once.
In TC, we used the temp hearing panels for every year up until this one as we paused our annual reassessment program while we convert to Tyler Tech's CAMA db.  When you make 25,000 changes, you
need more than 1 BAR.  This also allowed us to create a commercial, urban, and rural panel so that we had some specialization on each of those panels.
To get around this issue, I'd have 1 BAR member resign and then quickly appoint a qualified person.  But at this point, is there enough time to track someone (anyone) down to do it?  But it's
better than the alternative of using County staff to do it.

subject: RPSOnline
body:
Hello and Happy Friday!
Just wanted to pass along a very brief update on our progress with the launch of RPSO. I believe that because of our parcel size and fairly non-complex inventory we were an ideal first stop on this tour.
We are live in the production environment. As can be expected we are working through some conversion issues as we all know that RPS had its own unique set of quirks and challenges. We are also filtering through some need to haves vs. nice to haves with formats
and process flows. Understandably, things function differently from county to county and town to town and there will always be some of that in any migration.
Overall things are going well. I cannot speak highly enough of the response and dedication of the team working through this implementation. Hopefully our combined efforts will make your integrations a little smoother.
Best,
Barry

Lake Pleasant, NY 12108

body:

If the board of assessment review of any
assessing unit fails to meet for the purpose of hearing complaints or
stipulations in relation to assessments on the day specified by law, the
county treasurer, the chairman of the county legislative body and the
clerk of the county legislative body shall serve as an acting board of
assessment review which shall hear and determine complaints and ratify
stipulations in relation to assessments as provided in this section.

county treasurer, the chairman of the county legislative body and the
clerk of the county legislative body shall serve as an acting board of
assessment review which shall hear and determine complaints and ratify
stipulations in relation to assessments as provided in this section.

Subject: [EXTERNAL] Re: [External] Housing Trust
Hi Hannah,
Tompkins County got RPTL 467-j passed which is somewhat what they seem to describe (it's one of those population specific bills).  Under 467-j, the property is assessed normally.  But, each year, I get a
list from the housing trust of what the maximum resale value is for the improvement.  Typically, it goes up 2% per year or more if they do a capital improvement.  I then enter an exemption for the difference between the market value of the property and the
house owner's maximum resale value.
We have had this exemption in place since 2016 and have about 60 properties in this program.  For people in the program and the intent behind it, it's worthwhile.  I'm not a fan of the actual program as
the one it replaced was better in my opinion.  But I have no problem with this exemption - and the amount of work required is insignificant, but we have a great partner with our local housing trust provider.
Last year NYS offered RPTL 457-a as a local option to the rest of the state to allow a similar break but different.  This paints with a wider brush as it doesn't require the yearly work that 467-j requires.
Let me know if you have questions.
Thanks
Jay

Sent: Monday, June 1, 2026 6:52 PM
To: RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US <RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US>
Subject: BAR Quorum Question - Member Grieving Own Property
This message originated from outside of the organization.
Hi everyone,
A town has a three-member BAR, but only two members were present on Grievance Day. One of the BAR members filed a grievance on their own property and appropriately recused themselves from participating in the determination of that
complaint. However, with that recusal, only one BAR member remained available to hear the grievance, leaving the Board without the two-member quorum required to make a determination.
Has anyone dealt with this situation before or received guidance from ORPTS on how the grievance should be handled when a quorum cannot be achieved due to a required recusal? From what I found, we can either do an adjourned hearing if we can get the 3rd
BAR member to show up, or a 3 person panel of county officials would have to act as the BAR. Are those the only options? The town does not have any alternate or temporary member.
Thank you,
Victoria Blancato

Wyoming County

Good evening --
I hope that this message finds you safe and well.
My colleagues and I have received many great questions regarding the local option for a full property tax exemption for Veterans who have a 100% permanent and total VA rating. I imagine that these are questions shared by many advocates
across our state.
With these questions, I have compiled the below Q&A series for your review, based on what we know of this new tax exemption local option:
Q: I understand that TDIU is not required for the exemption. However, does it qualify for the total exemption?
A: No. A TDIU designation does not qualify. Only a 100% permanent and total VA disability compensation rating qualifies.
Q: If the Veteran held this new total tax exemption at the time of their passing, will their surviving spouse be able to continue receiving it?
A: If the Veteran holds this tax exemption at the time of their passing, the surviving spouse
will be able to continue to receive it after the Veteran passes away. The following language from Section 458-a, subsection (c), verifies this: "Where a veteran is also the unremarried surviving spouse of a veteran, such person may also receive any exemption
to which the deceased spouse was entitled."
Q: If a local government decides not to opt in to this new total exemption, will any of the existing Veterans property tax exemptions be impacted negatively?
A: No! Definitely not. If a local government decides not to opt in, there will be
no adverse impacts on any existing Veterans real property tax exemptions available in that locality.
Q: Does this apply to the Surviving Spouse of a Veteran who was 100% (not P&T)?
A: No. This would apply to the surviving spouse of a Veteran who had a 100% permanent and total rating from the VA, but
not the surviving spouse of a Veteran who had a 100% rating without a permanent and total designation from the VA.
Q: Is there a specific form for this exemption? Or will we use the standard 458rp and 458rp-dis?
A: There is no "special form" for this exemption. It is part of Section 458-a of the Real Property Tax Law, and thus the same forms that are used now for the Alternative Veterans Property Tax Exemption will still be used here.
Q: Is this the final edition of the bill that tax assessors will use in areas that opt in?
A: Barring any amendments that are unforeseen at this time, this will be the provision that is used by the property tax assessors based on taxable status occurring on and after October 1, 2026.
Q: This appears to include Veterans with qualifying conditions such as MST, PTSD, TBI who may not have received a fully honorable discharge, provided their discharge was not dishonorable or a bad conduct discharge. Is it fair to
understand the intent of this language as extending eligibility to Veterans whose discharge status may have been affected by difficult or mitigating circumstances, including qualifying conditions or prior policies affecting LGBT service members?
A: This language references the New York State Restoration of Honor Act. The Restoration of Honor Act provides a pathway to restore access to State benefits for Veterans who unjustly received a less-than-honorable administrative
separation due to their chain of command's misunderstanding of a mental health condition caused or worsened by military service, or due to laws or policies that discriminated against the Service Member's sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.
Among the State benefits that can be restored by a favorable Restoration of Honor Act decision is the Alternative Veterans Tax Exemption. As this new exemption is covered by the same state statute that governs the Alternative Veterans Tax
Exemption, a favorable Restoration of Honor Act decision can likewise open the door for the recipient Veteran to receive this new exemption as well, provided that they are in a locality that opts in and provided that they have a 100% permanent and total rating.
I hope that this helps. Please let me know if you have any follow-up questions, and I will be glad to answer them to the best of my ability.
As always, thank you for the advocacy that you provide for Veterans, Service Members, and Military Families every day.
Respectfully,

subject: Re: EXTERNAL Re: BAR Quorum Question - Member Grieving Own Property
body:
CAUTION:
I am not a lawyer and didn't sleep at a Holiday Inn last night...  But here is my take on this.
Super BAR or deny the application and send it to a SCAR hearing.
Because the BAR lacked a quorum the applications could be kicked to the super board (RPTL §527).
The BAR is a quasi-judicial body, governed by §41 of the General Construction Law.  The law requires a majority of the members, 2, to approve pass a motion/vote on the application.
If the BAR is unable to reach a majority decision, 2 votes, then the application is a functional denial.  In this case the BAR should deny the application and the property owner can proceed to a SCAR proceeding for further intervention if they want.
The best case scenario would be for the third member to get involved here.  See opinion 8-54 below.  He could review the minutes of the meeting and sit in on the decisions.
The BAR could further delay their deliberations until a time when the 3rd member is available.  It would need to be completed before final roll, but you could push it a week or two more.
Opinion 8-54 applies to the 3rd member stepping in to participate in the deliberations:
"A board member who is not present to hear a complaint, but later reviews the minutes of the hearing, may participate in the determination of the board with respect to that
complaint. This conclusion is based upon the decision in Taub v. Pirnie, 3 N.Y.2d 188, 144 N.E.2d 3, 165 N.Y.S.2d 1 (1957), where the Court of Appeals held that a member of the Village of Scarsdale Board of Appeals, who was not present at a hearing
with respect to an application for a zoning variance, could nonetheless vote on the application at a later meeting concerning same provided he had information sufficient to make an informed determination. This does not mean, however, that less than a majority
of the board may sit to hear complaints."
https://www.tax.ny.gov/pubs_and_bulls/orpts/legal_opinions/v8/54.htm

subject: Re: acting assessor
body:
CAUTION:
Actually it is a requirement
8188-2.2 Minimum qualification standards for appointed assessors.
(a) The minimum qualification standards for appointed assessors are as follows:
(1)
(i) graduation from high school, or possession of an accredited high school equivalency diploma; and
(ii) two years of satisfactory full-time paid experience in an occupation involving the valuation of real property, such as assessor, appraiser, valuation data manager, real property appraisal aide or the like. Such experience shall be deemed satisfactory if
it is demonstrated that the experience primarily was gained in the performance of one or more of the following tasks: collection and recording of property inventory data, preparation of comparable sales analysis reports, preparation of signed valuation or
appraisal estimates or reports using cost, income or market data approaches to value. Mere listing of real property for potential sale, or preparation of asking prices for real estate for potential sale, using multiple listing reports or other published asking
prices is not qualifying experience; or
(2) graduation from an accredited two-year college and one year of the experience described in subparagraph (1)(ii) of this subdivision; or
(3) graduation from an accredited four-year college and six months of the experience described in subparagraph (1)(ii) of this subdivision or graduation from an accredited four-year college and a written commitment from the county director that the county will
provide training in assessment administration, approved by ORPTS, within a six-month period; or
(4) certification by ORPTS as a candidate for assessor.

body:
CAUTION:
Morning all!
Has anyone run into the problem of an assessor not being able to attend Grievance Day due to an accident/illness and if so, how did they handle?
One of our municipalities has grievance day this upcoming Tuesday and the assessor is not able to attend and is not able to communicate with the municipality to designate a representative in their stead as far as I understand it.  Advice
I am receiving is to have the municipality designate someone to receive paperwork and schedule an adjourned hearing date for anyone that wants to be heard.
Trying to navigate still providing the claimant's rights and assessor's rights while possibly scheduling an adjourned "to be determined" hearing date.  I have also advised them to refer to their municipal attorney.  Looking at opinions
of counsel, I cannot find any clear guidance or example.
Thanks in advance for any guidance you may have!

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) Landlock Parcels
body:
CAUTION:
I would go with what Chris said, but, just to add, there is no true landlocked property in NY. Well, it's landlocked until the courts or government take care of it. Our NYS Constitution spells
this out in Article 1:
"[Compensation for taking private property; private roads; drainage of agricultural lands] §7. (a) Private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation.
(c) Private roads may be opened in the manner to be prescribed by law; but in every case the necessity of the road and the amount of all damage to be sustained by the opening thereof shall be first determined by a jury of freeholders, and such amount, together
with the expenses of the proceedings, shall be paid by the person to be benefitted."
You could always tell the owner that if you take it, you will have to build a private road through their property to the other one. It's an empty threat because that wouldn't make fiscal sense,
but it's a legit one.

To All:  We received an additional explanation regarding the veteran exemption option revised law- opting into this exemption would require the veteran to have not only a 100% disability rating,
but also a rating that specifically states it is 'total and permanent'.  As ratings can change each year, there may be towns that currently require yearly rating updates from the VA which probably should be done anyway regardless of this new option.  This
office is considering doing so as well. As far as our 'total and permanent' disabled veterans are concerned here in
XXXXXXX -which I believe this option is for, those veterans in that severe condition are residing in special military housing located within
XXXXXXX and are already tax exempt.
To All:  Please see below explanations of the newest iteration of the Veterans bill that was originally passed late last year (S.1183), revised in January (A.9448) and now again (S.9009-c Part EE) for the recent NYS budget.
The bottom line is if a veteran can prove a "total and permanent disability" from the VA (although he / she may be already getting a huge exemption now with the existing alternative veteran's exemption), and if the municipalities opt in,
veterans can receive a total tax exemption -even for special districts and school. You'll be hearing about this I'm sure.  Just to give you an idea of the impact, if every 100% rated veteran (98 in
XXXXXXX for 2026) would qualify, the town would be in the hole for an additional $440,000 (includes average special districts charges) and over $81,000 for the County. (Right now with the current veteran exemptions, the schools
are exempting about $60,000 in taxes and the Town and County about $100,000).  With this new option, the four school districts in general would be shifting almost $1 million additional tax dollars.  This is a serious concern and shift to other taxpayers even
when we offer a generous exemption already (A typical exemption now for a 100% rated vet is worth about $1,500 off for the town -plus they still pay special district charges- and roughly $900 off for school.  If adopted, this would also affect the Villages
that utilize our roll the following year. It makes little sense that the applicant would be eligible to avoid special district & use charges -  libraries, solid waste, fire, ambulance, hydrant, etc., but also their children would be subsidized as well for
essentially a free education. It appears that over the years, the VA has been very generous with their ratings as I would not characterize many of these applicants who walk in here after driving to town hall, "permanent and totally disabled."  This time the
legislature appears to have gone off the exemption cliff but unlike the second revision of the law, it is still an option to join or not to and which obviously is impactful if done so.  So although NYS is one of the highest taxed governments in the US (state
and local taxes) and people and businesses are leaving for more reasonable states, the legislature is making things even worse. Good luck with this option.

subject: Re: Special District question
body:

I would have pushed back on the town when I was calculating the tax rates last year.  I have had some last-minute districts get created but November/December is pushing it.  I also require a
copy of the resolution creating the district along with the map, plan, and report before adding the district to RPS.

subject: operating charges on farm
body:
CAUTION:
Hello all-
I had a Sanitary District ask me the question below- I asked for more clarification on the fees and she gave me the response below this-
Hi,
Considering the issues with Highland Pasture Poultry Farm Inc., non-renewal of discharge permit and lack of payment of monthly operating fees and penalties assessed in 2026
I am wondering how the District goes about relevying any unpaid bills onto the Annual Town/County Tax bills.
We have an annual levy and are made whole by turning over all unpaid bills to the Treasurer's Office each November but this facility is billed differently.  They are billed
monthly due to a discharge permit issued by the District.  Is there a procedure in place for this?
I look forward to hearing from you.
Diana Schwartz
Superintendent
Montgomery County
Sanitary District No.1
_____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
My question on type of charges:
Hi Christine,
No, the fee is not assessment based. This facility is a slaughterhouse.  Their monthly fee was determined by taking the Districts' actual expenditures from the prior year and determining what
it costs to treat each pound of Flow, BOD, TSS And FOGS (fats, oil and grease) and then setting an allowable limit.  The monthly fee remains the same for an entire year but when exceedances occur there is a formula used to assess a penalty.  An engineering
firm helped the District establish the language in the permit.
Hope that helps.
I have no idea is these can be relevied onto the County/Town bill--- I appreciate any help!!!!!!
Chris
Christine DePasquale
Director
Montgomery County Real Property
PO Box 1500
20 Park St.
Fonda, NY 12068
518-853-3996

body:
Some people who received this message don't often get email from kathleenkearney@onondaga.gov.
Learn why this is important
CAUTION:
Our county planned to adopt it for this year, but we passed it on March 3rd. We have changed exemptions later in the year in the past, and ORPTS guidance was "you probably shouldn't, but we're just attorneys for the state we can't tell you what to do" so our
attorney said that there was precedent to make this change for the 2026 roll, but this year it rubbed one of our assessors the wrong way and he went on a mission to force us to remove the exemption from the taxpayers after tentative roll.
He also posted a 2 page manifesto about it in the NYSAA bulletin. I apologize if this causes issues elsewhere (I had an email to y'all planned, but the CFO /CE are keeping things wrapped up until they decide how they want to handle it, so I held onto it). We
plan to go through the NYS legislature to get the change allowed so we can add it back before county/town bills.
Kathleen Kearney, Director

and totally disabled" but I assume the definition of that status by the VA says 100% disabled (thus "total" disability) so the guidance describes it that way.
Basically, semantics are weird?

Good evening --
I hope that this message finds you safe and well.
My colleagues and I have received many great questions regarding the local option for a full property tax exemption for Veterans who have a 100% permanent and total VA rating. I imagine that these are questions shared by many advocates
across our state.
With these questions, I have compiled the below Q&A series for your review, based on what we know of this new tax exemption local option:
Q: I understand that TDIU is not required for the exemption. However, does it qualify for the total exemption?
A: No. A TDIU designation does not qualify. Only a 100% permanent and total VA disability compensation rating qualifies.
Q: If the Veteran held this new total tax exemption at the time of their passing, will their surviving spouse be able to continue receiving it?
A: If the Veteran holds this tax exemption at the time of their passing, the surviving spouse
will be able to continue to receive it after the Veteran passes away. The following language from Section 458-a, subsection (c), verifies this: "Where a veteran is also the unremarried surviving spouse of a veteran, such person may also receive any exemption
to which the deceased spouse was entitled."
Q: If a local government decides not to opt in to this new total exemption, will any of the existing Veterans property tax exemptions be impacted negatively?
A: No! Definitely not. If a local government decides not to opt in, there will be
no adverse impacts on any existing Veterans real property tax exemptions available in that locality.
Q: Does this apply to the Surviving Spouse of a Veteran who was 100% (not P&T)?
A: No. This would apply to the surviving spouse of a Veteran who had a 100% permanent and total rating from the VA, but
not the surviving spouse of a Veteran who had a 100% rating without a permanent and total designation from the VA.
Q: Is there a specific form for this exemption? Or will we use the standard 458rp and 458rp-dis?
A: There is no "special form" for this exemption. It is part of Section 458-a of the Real Property Tax Law, and thus the same forms that are used now for the Alternative Veterans Property Tax Exemption will still be used here.
Q: Is this the final edition of the bill that tax assessors will use in areas that opt in?
A: Barring any amendments that are unforeseen at this time, this will be the provision that is used by the property tax assessors based on taxable status occurring on and after October 1, 2026.
Q: This appears to include Veterans with qualifying conditions such as MST, PTSD, TBI who may not have received a fully honorable discharge, provided their discharge was not dishonorable or a bad conduct discharge. Is it fair to
understand the intent of this language as extending eligibility to Veterans whose discharge status may have been affected by difficult or mitigating circumstances, including qualifying conditions or prior policies affecting LGBT service members?
A: This language references the New York State Restoration of Honor Act. The Restoration of Honor Act provides a pathway to restore access to State benefits for Veterans who unjustly received a less-than-honorable administrative
separation due to their chain of command's misunderstanding of a mental health condition caused or worsened by military service, or due to laws or policies that discriminated against the Service Member's sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.
Among the State benefits that can be restored by a favorable Restoration of Honor Act decision is the Alternative Veterans Tax Exemption. As this new exemption is covered by the same state statute that governs the Alternative Veterans
Tax Exemption, a favorable Restoration of Honor Act decision can likewise open the door for the recipient Veteran to receive this new exemption as well, provided that they are in a locality that opts in and provided that they have a 100% permanent and total
rating.
I hope that this helps. Please let me know if you have any follow-up questions, and I will be glad to answer them to the best of my ability.
As always, thank you for the advocacy that you provide for Veterans, Service Members, and Military Families every day.
Respectfully,
Benjamin P. Pomerance

Subject: Re: Homeowner Bill of Rights in Article 11 RPTL
The Homeowner bill of rights only applies to residential property owners for their primary residence.  I believe in my county we send the homeowner warning notice to everyone though
because it's easier administratively.  However, surplus funds can be claimed for any type of property.
Real Property Tax
§  1197.  Claims  for surplus.
1. Any person who had any right, title,
interest, claim, lien or equity  of  redemption  in  or
upon  a  parcel
immediately  prior  to  the  issuance of the judgment of
foreclosure may
file a claim with the court
having  jurisdiction  for  a  share  of  any
surplus  resulting  from the sale of such property. Such claims shall be
administered and adjudicated, and such surplus shall be distributed,  in
the  same  manner  as  in  an action to foreclose a mortgage pursuant to
article thirteen of the  real  property  actions  and  proceedings  law,
subject to the provisions of this section.
2.  (a)  Where the property was sold by a public sale, the amount paid
for the property shall be accepted as the full value of the property. No
party may maintain a claim for surplus or  any  other  claim  or  action
against  the  tax  district  on  the  basis that the amount paid for the
property did not fairly represent the property's value.
(b) Where the property was  sold  by  other  than  a  public  sale,  a
claimant  may  make  a motion, upon notice to the enforcing officer, for
the surplus to be recalculated on the basis  that  the  property's  full
value  on  the  date of the sale was substantially higher than the value
used to measure the surplus pursuant to subparagraph (ii)  of  paragraph
(a)  of  subdivision  one  of  section eleven hundred ninety-six of this
title. If the court or its referee finds that  a  preponderance  of  the
evidence  supports  the  claimant's  position,  the court may direct the
enforcing officer to recalculate the surplus based upon  the  property's
value  as  determined  by  the  court  or referee. The court may further
direct the enforcing officer to pay the  difference  into  court  to  be
distributed as required by this section.
3.  Where  the  court  has  appointed  a  referee  to preside over the
proceedings pursuant to subdivision  two  of  section  thirteen  hundred
sixty-one of the real property actions and proceedings law, it shall not
be  necessary for such referee to make a report of such proceedings; nor
shall it be necessary for the court to confirm  by  order  or  otherwise
such proceedings.
4.
In  the  case  of  residential  property,  if  at  the time of the
confirmation of the report of sale, no  former  homeowner
has  filed  a
claim  for  surplus,  and  there  are surplus proceeds
that remain to be
distributed, the proceeding shall remain open for at least
three  years
from  the  confirmation of the report of sale, or for such
longer period
as the court may direct.
If a former homeowner should file a  claim  for
surplus  during  such  period, the court shall proceed as if it had been
timely filed.
5. At the conclusion of such proceedings, any surplus funds that  have
not  been claimed shall be deemed abandoned but shall be paid to the tax
district, not to the state comptroller, and shall be  used  by  the  tax
district to reduce its tax levy.
6.  To  the  extent  the  provisions  of  article thirteen of the real
property  actions  and  proceedings  law  are  inconsistent   with   the
provisions of this article, the provisions of this article shall govern.
Jennifer Indelicato, CCD
Cayuga County Director of Real Property Serivces
160 Genesee St., 5th Floor
Auburn, NY 13021

title. If the court or its referee finds that  a  preponderance  of  the
evidence  supports  the  claimant's  position,  the court may direct the
enforcing officer to recalculate the surplus based upon  the  property's
value  as  determined  by  the  court  or referee. The court may further
direct the enforcing officer to pay the  difference  into  court  to  be
distributed as required by this section.
3.  Where  the  court  has  appointed  a  referee  to preside over the
proceedings pursuant to subdivision  two  of  section  thirteen  hundred
sixty-one of the real property actions and proceedings law, it shall not
be  necessary for such referee to make a report of such proceedings; nor
shall it be necessary for the court to confirm  by  order  or  otherwise
such proceedings.
4.
In  the  case  of  residential  property,  if  at  the time of the
confirmation of the report of sale, no  former  homeowner
has  filed  a
claim  for  surplus,  and  there  are surplus proceeds
that remain to be
distributed, the proceeding shall remain open for at least
three  years
from  the  confirmation of the report of sale, or for such
longer period
as the court may direct.
If a former homeowner should file a  claim  for
surplus  during  such  period, the court shall proceed as if it had been
timely filed.
5. At the conclusion of such proceedings, any surplus funds that  have
not  been claimed shall be deemed abandoned but shall be paid to the tax
district, not to the state comptroller, and shall be  used  by  the  tax
district to reduce its tax levy.
6.  To  the  extent  the  provisions  of  article thirteen of the real
property  actions  and  proceedings  law  are  inconsistent   with   the
provisions of this article, the provisions of this article shall govern.

subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] [*Suspicious URL*] 471 - Surviving Spouse of PO Killed in Line of Duty
body:
CAUTION:
Good morning, Trish,
I believe that there is a definition somewhere stating that for NYS taxation purposes a spouse is someone married to another, and that if they remarry then they are no longer the spouse of that person
because they are the spouse of someone else.
So, according to that, being a spouse survives death, but not remarriage. And by that definition, we do not need to put "unremarried" in our resolution or law before the word "spouse," as not being
remarried is implied. Or something along those lines; I cannot find the reference that my county attorney's office had found and am only on my second cup of coffee.
I think maybe it was from the Department of Redundancy Department...

subject: Article 7 or COE
body:

Learn why this is important
CAUTION:
Good morning -
One of my assessors did a town reassessment this year. An owner of a newly built commercial property came to her for an informal hearing. He did not have much to support his case, mostly just compared it to some of his other properties,
so she did not lower the assessment He filled out the RP-524 and left it with her for grievance.
He did not end up showing up on grievance day, so the BAR reviewed what he had left with the assessor, and also determined
not to lower his assessment.
Now he has contacted the assessor, stating that he just noticed that the square footage is incorrect on the new building. The assessor looked into it and discovered that the square footage
is indeed overstated (listing almost double from what it actually is).
The owner is hoping the assessor can submit a COE (RP-553), as opposed to having to file an Article 7.
So, here is my question - is this correctable? I am not seeing a valid correctable error reason that would fit, as the assessor did not have this info in her records before, and just became aware of the discrepancy now.
If you would recommend a correction, what reason would you use? Or would you say that it is a clear grievable issue, and the owner needs to file an Article 7, if he wishes to pursue it more?
Thank you for any input!!!
~ Meghan.
Meghan K. Kincaid
Director for Real Property Tax Services
Yates County

CAUTION:
Looping back to this question.
The text of 471 does not specifically state "unremarried surviving spouse" as a qualification for the exemption.  The legislative summary refers
to widows/widowers but nothing about unremarried surviving spouses.
I think that this exemption would be kept in place for a remarried surviving spouse.

Good morning, Trish,
I believe that there is a definition somewhere stating that for NYS taxation purposes a spouse is someone married to another, and that if they remarry then they are no longer the spouse of that person because they are the spouse of someone
else.
So, according to that, being a spouse survives death, but not remarriage. And by that definition, we do not need to put "unremarried" in our resolution or law before the word "spouse," as not being remarried is implied. Or something along
those lines; I cannot find the reference that my county attorney's office had found and am only on my second cup of coffee.
I think maybe it was from the Department of Redundancy Department...

<p style="border:1px; border-style:solid; border-color: #FFCACA; line-height:10.0pt; background: #FFEA89; padding: 1em;">
<b><span style="font-size:10.0pt; color:#C50509">NOTICE:</span></b><span style="font-size:10.0pt; color:black"> This email originated from
<b><u>outside</u></b> of Onondaga County's email system. <b>Use caution</b> with links and attachments.
</span></p>
<div>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>NYS Real Property Tax Law §471</b></div>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>Surviving Spouse Exemption for Police Officers Killed in the Line of Duty</b></div>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>Overview</b></div>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
New York’s Real Property Tax Law §471 provides a <b>50% property tax exemption</b> for the
<b>primary residence</b> of a <b>surviving spouse of a police officer killed in the line of duty</b>, if the local government or school district adopts the exemption by local law or resolution.</div>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
This summary consolidates the <b>exact statutory text</b> of RPTL §471 and the controlling definition of
<b>“surviving spouse”</b> from EPTL §5‑1.2, which determines eligibility—including the effect of remarriage.</div>
<hr>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>1. Exact Text: Real Property Tax Law §471</b></div>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>Source: NewYork.Public.Law</b></div>
<blockquote class="elementToProof">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>“§ 471 Surviving spouses of police officers killed in the line of duty</b></div>
<ol start="1">
<li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
After the local legislative body of a county, city, town, or village passes a local law, or a school district passes a resolution, notwithstanding any other provision of law,
<b>real property owned by a surviving spouse of a police officer killed in the line of duty, and constituting the primary residence of such surviving spouse shall be exempt from taxation to the extent of fifty per centum of the assessed valuation thereof.</b> Within
such local law or resolution, the local legislative body or school district may reduce the percentage of exemption authorized pursuant to this section.</div>
</li><li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
As used in this section, the term “police officer” shall have the same meaning as defined in section 1.20 of the criminal procedure law.”</div>
</li></ol>
</blockquote>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>Important:</b> §471 does <b>not</b> define “surviving spouse.” New York law requires using the definition in the Estates, Powers & Trusts Law (EPTL) when a statute uses that term without defining it.</div>
<hr>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>2. Exact Text: EPTL §5‑1.2 — Disqualification as Surviving Spouse</b></div>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>Source: FindLaw (NY Consolidated Laws)</b></div>
<blockquote class="elementToProof">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>“§ 5‑1.2 Disqualification as surviving spouse</b> (a) A husband or wife is a <b>
surviving spouse</b> within the meaning, and for the purposes of 4‑1.1, 5‑1.1, 5‑1.1‑A, 5‑1.3, 5‑3.1 and 5‑4.4,
<b>unless it is established satisfactorily to the court having jurisdiction of the action or proceeding that:</b></div>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
(1) <i>A final decree or judgment of divorce, of annulment or declaring the nullity of a marriage or dissolving such marriage on the ground of absence, recognized as valid under the law of this state, was in effect when the deceased spouse died.</i></div>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
(2) <i>The marriage was void as incestuous under section five of the domestic relations law, bigamous under section six thereof, or a
</i><b><i>prohibited remarriage</i></b><i> under section eight thereof.</i></div>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>3. How the Two Statutes Work Together</b></div>
<ul data-tight="true">
<li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
RPTL §471 grants the exemption only to a <b>“surviving spouse of a police officer killed in the line of duty.”</b></div>
</li><li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
Because §471 does <b>not</b> define the term, the EPTL definition applies automatically.</div>
</li><li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
Under New York law, a person is a “surviving spouse” <b>only while they remain unmarried after the officer’s death</b>.</div>
</li><li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
<b>Remarriage ends eligibility</b>, because the individual is no longer the surviving spouse
<i>of the deceased officer</i>.</div>
</li><li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
This rule is consistent across all NY survivor‑based exemptions (military, volunteer firefighter, etc.).</div>
</li></ul>
<hr>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>4. Practical Implications</b></div>
<ul data-tight="true">
<li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
Eligibility ends at the <b>next taxable status date</b> after remarriage.</div>
</li><li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
Local assessors may require notification of any change in marital status.</div>
</li><li style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em;" role="presentation" class="elementToProof">
The exemption applies only if adopted by the <b>county, town, village, or school district</b>.</div>
</li></ul>
<hr>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
<b>5. Key Takeaway</b></div>
<div style="margin-top: 1em; margin-bottom: 1em; font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">
The exemption under RPTL §471 applies <b>only while the applicant remains the unremarried surviving spouse</b> of the fallen police officer. Remarriage legally ends the status of “surviving spouse,” and therefore ends the exemption.</div>
<div style="font-family: Aptos, Aptos_EmbeddedFont, Aptos_MSFontService, Calibri, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: 12pt; color: rgb(0, 0, 0);" class="elementToProof">

subject: Re: Battery storage under RPTL 487
body:
CAUTION:
Good afternoon everyone,
Thank you for this information Paul!
What are everyone's thoughts on the impact of the Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) on the State's 2026 Solar/Wind Valuation Model?  When I add BESS systems to the model they seem to be significantly reduced (70-90% decrease in value) as compared to
a system without BESS.
If there is already another email chain on this, then please let me know.  I did not see one when I did a quick search.
Have a wonderful day and a Happy Independence Day,
Alex
Alexander W. Marchenkoff, Director
Jefferson County Real Property Tax Services
175 Arsenal St, 3rd Floor
Watertown, NY 13601
315-785-3190
amarchenkoff@jeffersoncountyny.gov
On Wed, May 20, 2026 at 12:55 PM Wiley, Paul <00000010df4a36f7-dmarc-request@list-nysac.us> wrote:
Hey all,
I had thought that battery storage had to be in conjunction with a solar or other alternative energy source to get a PILOT under 487, but in re-reading the law, it looks like battery storage connected to the grid is eligible for a PILOT
even without being part of a solar project, because it says "or" below. Am I reading that right?
"Real property that contains a solar energy, wind energy, farm waste energy, micro-hydroelectric energy, fuel cell electric generating, micro-combined heat and power generating equipment, or an electric energy storage system approved by
the State Energy Research and Development Authority is exempt from taxation for a period of 15 years to the extent of any increase in assessed value due to the system. Such property is liable for special ad valorem levies and special assessments. The exemption
as reenacted in 1990 is subject to local option."
https://www.tax.ny.gov/research/property/assess/manuals/vol4/pt1/sec4_01/sec487.htm
We have some battery storage connected to solar projects that are part of PILOTs done before I started here, and we have three battery storage projects that went through our IDA to get IDA PILOTs (still not happy about that, but I have
been able to contain my anger into a slow simmer, so I have that going for me). But we have not had any battery projects asking for 487 PILOTs-- until now.
And what rate are you all doing battery storage? We had done the solar ones at $4,000 per MW of storage, compared to the $10,000 per MW that we get for solar (Central Hudson and Orange & Rockland have some of the highest rates this side
of Hawaii, so it justifies the high PILOT rates. Don't at me, y'all).
Paul Wiley
Director
Orange County Office of Real Property
255 Main St
Goshen, NY 10924
O: (845) 291-2494
C: (845) 806-0817

subject: Land Owned by Housing Trust
body:
CAUTION:
I have already spoken with Tompkins County regarding this issue, as they have an exemption to handle these kinds of parcels, but I am curious how other counties deal with this.
We have a housing trust that sells homes to low-income families. Only the improvements are transferred, while the housing trust retains ownership of the land. There is some kind of land lease agreement between the homeowner and the trust, whether they pay $10
a year for this lease, I have no clue. There are deed restrictions in place limiting the homeowner on future sale price.
Does anyone have something similar, where a not-for-profit retains ownership of the land? If so, could they apply for an exemption on the land value, considering they are a not-for-profit? There are issues rising regarding the assessments of these parcels and
I am trying to gather as much information as possible before a meeting on Thursday.
Thank you,

subject: Ag Inclusion Applicants
body:
CAUTION:
Hello,
Is it required by law that the Ag Board notify the towns if there are Ag inclusion applicants in their town each year?  Or is this a courtesy?
Two of our towns are saying that we should be sending letters to the neighboring homes to an applicant, notifying them of the public hearing.  A particular
councilman has taken this on as a full-time job and has written to an Ag & Markets attorney, when our County Attorney told him that we are not required to do this, and the Ag & Markets attorney told him, NO, this would not be appropriate for the Ag Board to
do.  They are required to advertise the public hearing, but that's it.  He is now arguing with this attorney that Ag Boards should be required to do this, and that the law should be changed.  This all began because we notified our towns that there were applicants
in their towns, and when the public hearing was.  Two towns went and sent letters to all surrounding homeowners to the applicants, and it caused a firestorm for one applicant, who the neighbor had no problem with prior, but now this ag inclusion notice made
them think that she is going to start some commercial equestrian center (she is a small, new horse farm, beautifully set and laid out with care, with 11 stalls that she does some boarding with, and has a small riding ring.  She is a rider and competitor herself).
She will be doing nothing different--just wanted to get into the district.
Is it required that the Board notifies the town of the applicants, as we have done since I've been here, or has this been a courtesy that we have been doing?
Thanks, T
Trish McLoughlin
Director  ● Office of Real Property Tax Services
PHONE | 845.808.1000 ● X-49315 | WEBSITE |

PUTNAM COUNTY GOVERNMENT NEW YORK

3. The county legislative body shall hold a public hearing upon giving
notice in the following manner:
a. The notice of public hearing shall contain a statement that one or
more requests for inclusion of predominantly viable agricultural land
within a certified agricultural district have been filed with the county
legislative body pursuant to this section; identify the land, generally,
proposed to be included; indicate the time, date and place of the public
hearing, which shall occur after receipt of the report of the county
agricultural and farmland protection board; and include a statement that
the hearing shall be held to consider the request or requests and
recommendations of the county agricultural and farmland protection
board.
b.
The notice shall be published in a newspaper having a general
circulation within the county and
shall be given in writing directly to
those municipalities whose territory encompasses the lands which are
proposed to be included in an agricultural district and to the
commissioner.

Subject: Ag Inclusion Applicants
Hello,
Is it required by law that the Ag Board notify the towns if there are Ag inclusion applicants in their town each year?  Or is this a courtesy?
Two of our towns are saying that we should be sending letters to the neighboring homes to an applicant, notifying them of the public hearing.  A particular
councilman has taken this on as a full-time job and has written to an Ag & Markets attorney, when our County Attorney told him that we are not required to do this, and the Ag & Markets attorney told him, NO, this would not be appropriate for the Ag Board to
do.  They are required to advertise the public hearing, but that's it.  He is now arguing with this attorney that Ag Boards should be required to do this, and that the law should be changed.  This all began because we notified our towns that there were applicants
in their towns, and when the public hearing was.  Two towns went and sent letters to all surrounding homeowners to the applicants, and it caused a firestorm for one applicant, who the neighbor had no problem with prior, but now this ag inclusion notice made
them think that she is going to start some commercial equestrian center (she is a small, new horse farm, beautifully set and laid out with care, with 11 stalls that she does some boarding with, and has a small riding ring.  She is a rider and competitor herself).
She will be doing nothing different--just wanted to get into the district.
Is it required that the Board notifies the town of the applicants, as we have done since I've been here, or has this been a courtesy that we have been doing?
Thanks, T
Trish McLoughlin

subject: Re: VRBO & SCAR
body:
In order to qualify for small claims the property must be an owner occupied one, two or three family residence.  It can be a seasonal residence as long as the owner occupies it during that time.  I have made a motion to dismiss at a hearing based on the fact that the property was not owner occupied and the hearing officer granted the dismissal.  I guess they could try, but be prepared to prove that they aren't occupying the property and also be prepared to prove the value in the case the hearing officer won't grant the dismissal.
Dawn Allen, CCD

Suite #1
Albion, NY 14411

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) RP-553 Notice of Determination
body:
CAUTION:
Why not just send the completed 553 after it gets signed off by the BAR? The owner gets an unsigned one ahead of time, and then the BAR signs it after meeting again. It shows the new assessment. I guess if
the BAR denies it for some reason then more explanation is needed, but they are not supposed to deny them.
This is how we do it in our assessing towns. Those we don't assess for, I never see the outcomes of their 553s. We just do what the new statement of changes show.

subject: Re: School district aquires house
body:
CAUTION:
The school will have to pay the taxes on the property until the next roll year.  They are not one of the entities that are immediately tax exempt.  Opinions of Counsel
1-97 covers this, it reads, in part:
One exception to this rule is provided by section 494 of the Real Property Tax Law. The provisions of section 494 apply only in a city having a population of one million or more and in the County of Westchester.
In brief, section 494 makes formerly exempt real property taxable pro rata for the unexpired portion of a fiscal year where after taxable status date such property is acquired by or transferred to any person, association or corporation not entitled to an exemption.
It should be noted that taxable property acquired after taxable status date by a person or organization eligible for exemption would continue to be fully taxable until the next assessment roll is prepared,
and the provisions of this section would be impractical of operation in the various towns of the State where there are no year-round tax collectors.
Candy Akin, CCD
Real Property Tax Director
2025-2026 President, NYSACDRPTS

M: 315-907-2032

subject: Re: Special District-Type "E"
body:
CAUTION:
Hi Kristen:
This may help. I used the HELP button on V4 ( it's my best friend lol) , looked under Special Districts, and this is what it states:
Type special district code or select from drop down selection. Edits are performed if data is incorrect or incomplete.
Data options:
Special District Code: a user-defined five position alphanumeric code created in response for a particular taxing unit service.
Primary Units: the number of primary units for the parcel.
Secondary Units: the number of secondary units for the parcel.
Percent: what portion of the parcel or part of the assessment is located in the special district.
Initial Year: the year when the special district began for that parcel.
Type: indicates what information is recorded in the Value field.  Valid codes are 'T' (pre-calculated tax); 'S' (allows user entered value other than Total AV - exemptions would apply); and 'E' (allows user entered value other than Total AV
- exemptions would not apply.).
Value: the override value of a special district in conjunction with an 'E' or 'S' type.
Move Tax: the dollar/cent value attributed to the parcel.
Click save, , on the toolbar.
Update a Special District:
Select Special District from the tree view.
Click on the special district to be changed in the list area (top area of the special district screen).
Change data in the detail area (bottom area of screen).
Click save, , on the toolbar.
Delete a Special District:
Select Special District from the tree view.
Click on the special district to be deleted in the list area.
Click trash, , on the toolbar.
Click save, , on the toolbar.
Hope this helps you out, but would make sense as to why they are lower. Have a great day! 🙂

subject: 100% Vet Taxes and Special Districts
body:
CAUTION:
I had a meeting with a couple of Veteran Services Directors and my counterpart in Wyoming County (hey Vicky) yesterday. We are trying to get on the same page for how we want to write-up our local laws. One question came up about the vet
being exempt from special district and special assessments. The new law reads:
"shall be fully exempt from taxation and special district charges, assessments and special ad valorem levies"
What do we take this to truly mean? Are they exempt from all special districts that were legally formed? That could be garbage, snow removal, light, water, sewer, fire, etc. Then they are also exempt from any time a muni puts in a huge
water line and pays for it through a special assessment? How about those charges that are billed outside of a special district? For instance, if a muni bills their water/sewer separately but then has to relevy an unpaid bill?
I'm thinking that they are exempt from everything other then relevies for bills outside a district (like usage perhaps).
Daniel T. Martonis, CCD
Director of Real Property Tax Services
Chair, Cattaraugus County Land Bank
Board Chair, NYSACDRPTS
Cattaraugus County
Real Property Tax Services
207 Rock City Street, Suite 101
Little Valley, NY 14755
Phone: (716) 938-2324
Fax: (716) 938-2758

subject: Re: EXTERNAL 100% Vet Taxes and Special Districts
body:
CAUTION:
Dan I am on the same page.  I believe they are exempt from all special district taxes including fire, ambulance, light, drainage, etc.  I also believe that they would be exempt from sewer/water
capital expenses associated with the district maintenance and expansion where applicable.
I concur with your position on the usage charges for water/sewer.  They are responsible for those as they are fees not taxes.  I would expand this to include maintenance fees associated with
snow removal, grass cutting, garbage collection, etc.  I would also group fees associated with code mandated work/demolitions here.  IMO they are liable for these charges/fees.
Michael McGuire, IAO, CCD
Director
Albany County Real Property Tax Service Agency
112 State Street, Room 1103, Albany, NY 12207
tel   518 487-5292  fax  518 447-2503
Michael.McGuire@albanycountyny.gov

I had a meeting with a couple of Veteran Services Directors and my counterpart in Wyoming County (hey Vicky) yesterday. We are trying to get on the same page for
how we want to write-up our local laws. One question came up about the vet being exempt from special district and special assessments. The new law reads:
"shall be fully exempt from taxation and special district charges, assessments and special ad valorem levies"
What do we take this to truly mean? Are they exempt from all special districts that were legally formed? That could be garbage, snow removal, light, water, sewer,
fire, etc. Then they are also exempt from any time a muni puts in a huge water line and pays for it through a special assessment? How about those charges that are billed outside of a special district? For instance, if a muni bills their water/sewer separately
but then has to relevy an unpaid bill?
I'm thinking that they are exempt from everything other then relevies for bills outside a district (like usage perhaps).

subject: Re: C-PACE
body:
CAUTION:
We have had Energize NY for years and we have a local law for C-PACE.  We 2 parcels that are participating in the Energize NY program which from my 30 seconds of research seem like they are similar
programs.
Basically, the property owner gets their loan from the state.  Then before we process County/Town bills, we get a report from the state with the parcels and how much is owed on the loan for the
year.  We add that amount as a move tax to the parcel.  The town turns the money over to the county and then the county turns it over to the state.  When we first got it, I thought it was going to be a nightmare, but it hasn't really been a big deal for my
office.  Again this is the Energize NY program and C-PACE could be a little different.
