Subject: COE question
Good Morning...
I have an assessor that has requested a COE for a property that has a permit for construction of a seasonal residence.  The permit was issued 2024.  The assessor checked
the open permits in February 25 and, without an onsite inspection, increased the AV as if the structure was 100% complete.  A change of assessment notice was sent to the property owner by the assessor.  The property owner did not question the new AV, file
a grievance or even call the assessor until the school tax bill was received.
At that point in time the assessor went through a checklist of percentage complete with the property owner and has since determined the construction is only 6% complete.
The assessor is asking for a COE based on Error in Essential Fact.
I'm looking at this as the property owner should have filed a grievance or at a minimum contacted the assessor about the increase in AV.  The assessor is looking at
it as she made an error.  Obviously there was no taxable status review done.
So, what do all of you think?  Is this correctable under Essential Fact or not?
Thanks

Good Morning...
I have an assessor that has requested a COE for a property that has a permit for construction of a seasonal residence.  The permit was issued 2024.  The assessor checked
the open permits in February 25 and, without an onsite inspection, increased the AV as if the structure was 100% complete.  A change of assessment notice was sent to the property owner by the assessor.  The property owner did not question the new AV, file
a grievance or even call the assessor until the school tax bill was received.
At that point in time the assessor went through a checklist of percentage complete with the property owner and has since determined the construction is only 6% complete.
The assessor is asking for a COE based on Error in Essential Fact.
I'm looking at this as the property owner should have filed a grievance or at a minimum contacted the assessor about the increase in AV.  The assessor is looking at it
as she made an error.  Obviously there was no taxable status review done.
So, what do all of you think?  Is this correctable under Essential Fact or not?
Thanks

body:
I'll add in my two cents...you could correct it if you want, or you could call it valuation. If you correct it you could use 3(b) since the improvement wasn't in existence.
This one is a gray area for me. I've had assessors that never visit the property and don't mail out the increase letters (shocking, I know). Those I tend to lean towards the property owner on. If I know that
the property was visited and every letter was sent out and ignored, then I won't do the correction.
Of course if you do the correction then the assessor will never learn from their mistake and will continue to not visit new builds.
Good luck.

body:
Hello,
I had a co-op community's Star Savings get dropped off of their single main bill that they get, when I merged my databases.  I have manually added the Star
exemptions and re-ran the roll, just for the purpose of producing a new, correct bill for them (and to make sure it matched my correction spreadsheet).  They had already paid their bill to the school district, so I filled out an RP-556.  The refund amount

To: RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US
Subject: Re: Village Dissolving
Approximately ten years ago, we had a village within our jurisdiction formally dissolve. At the time, the village carried outstanding debt related to former village
employees' health insurance. To address this, we established a special district, applied solely to the parcels within the former village boundaries. This ensured that only those properties remained responsible for the associated debt.
The State provided us with a script to update the database accordingly, which included modifying the SWIS codes--not just for the former village parcels, but also
for the affected town parcels.
Lastly, while not required, we recommend that any similar actions be taken with appropriate legal oversight. We made it clear at the time that we did not want to
be held responsible should someone fail to follow proper legal procedure. Conducting due diligence is a matter of preference, but it helps avoid complications down the road.

Approximately ten years ago, we had a village within our jurisdiction formally dissolve. At the time, the village carried outstanding debt related to former village employees' health insurance. To address this, we established a special district, applied solely to the parcels within the former village boundaries. This ensured that only those properties remained responsible for the associated debt.
The State provided us with a script to update the database accordingly, which included modifying the SWIS codes--not just for the former village parcels, but also for the affected town parcels.
Lastly, while not required, we recommend that any similar actions be taken with appropriate legal oversight. Conducting due diligence is a matter of preference, but it helps avoid complications down the road.

subject: Re: Village Dissolving
body:
We had a Village dissolve on 1/1/24. The State gave us a script to convert all of printkeys. The Town absorbed all of the payments/debts. The only issue we
had was that the 2024 Town and County bill still said Village because of the timing. People questioned that. For our tax mapping we changed all of the SWIS numbers, deleted the Village boundary and gave a list to the Assessor. We kept all of the same SBLs
that the Village had. For our history cards we hand changed those. We updated our online information- anywhere that said Village (we still find some places)
Otherwise it went smoothly. It was not at all how hard we thought it would be.

Friday, September 19, 2025. After that, you
might still snag a room at the government rate, but no promises--so if you like having an actual place to sleep, book now.
For those rolling in on Sunday (10/19), we're starting with a Zombie Walk from
7-8 PM. Dinner is on us from 5:30-6:30 PM, and the networking suite in the Board Room will be open all evening. Cathy will be cooking
up s'mores both Sunday and Monday nights at the fire ring on the porch of the networking suite--because nothing says "professional conference" like sticky fingers and open flame.
Monday night (10/20) is our haunted house adventure from
7-8 PM. Costumes aren't just encouraged, they're basically mandatory. Bring your best look because there's a costume contest with prizes--and
trust me, you want those bragging rights.
And on Tuesday (10/21), ORPTS will be on site demoing RPS Online. The setup will be right next to our conference room, so yes--you can casually "sneak out" of the ethics class to take a peek at RPSO. We won't
tell.
So book your room, pack your Halloween finest, and get ready for a conference that's equal parts business and boos.
See you soon,
Michael McGuire, IAO, CCD

I am apparently mean to my assessors.  Our cut off is November 15th each year.  I do extend it in very specific circumstances.  For instance, this year, I just had 130
parcel settlement and that was lowering the AV over $100,000,000.  The judge just signed the orders so we are working on getting everything updated.

senders or unexpected emails.
Good morning, all -
So, I have my county equalization and apportionment spreadsheet basically done, just waiting until our public hearing and adoption of the county's budget to get the levy. SCAR decisions are done for this year,
so, barring any corrections of error, or the off-chance that an Article 7 that is hanging out there fiiinally settles, I am good to go. Or so I thought.
Just heard from one of my town assessors that an Article 7 case in her town DID just settle. I asked her to send me a copy. She did, but it isn't signed - not by the petitioner, the assessor, and, most significantly,
not the judge.
So, I am trying to track down an official signed order.
It got me to thinking though... Do you have a cut-off date that you will make changes to your file for Article 7 or SCAR decisions when working on town & county processing? It would be great to get the correct
amount on the town and county tax bill, but changes alter the town and county rates, my apportionment spreadsheet, etc, so there I have to draw the line at some point.
Anyway, let me know if you have a cut-off date, or if it varies year-to-year.
Thanks so much,
Meghan.

subject: Guidance Needed on Handling Subdivision Not Reflected on 2025 Assessment Roll
body:
Hi everyone,
We have a property where a portion of vacant land was sold in September 2024. Due to an error with the deed/survey map, the subdivision was not processed in our system in time for the taxable status date, so the parcel was not split on
the 2025 assessment roll. As a result:
The new owner of the subdivided portion has not received a school tax bill.The previous owner of the original parcel is being taxed on the entire acreage.
I'm looking for guidance on the best way to handle this. My current thinking is to file an RP-556 to refund the original owner for the school taxes. At this point, I would prefer not to make any changes to the roll before the town/county
bills so I would also do a correction afterward for original owner to the town/county tax roll. Would the proper approach then be to treat the amount the new owner should have paid as omits next year?
Thank you!
Victoria Blancato
Director, Real Property Tax Services
Wyoming County
143 North Main Street, Warsaw, NY 14569
Phone: (585) 786-8828 | Email: vblancato@wyomingcountyny.gov
https://www.wyomingcountyny.gov/

subject: Re: Guidance Needed on Handling Subdivision Not Reflected on 2025 Assessment Roll
body:
Tori -
Just a thought...if the parties are not willing to work things out amongst themselves for school you may run into an issue for an omit next year.  If you do an apportionment for town and county you are not correcting anything.  If there is no error being corrected on the tax or assessment rolls this year, I'm not sure how that could turn into an omit for school taxes next year?
If they cannot work out the school bill and you end up having to do a refund for school it would make sense to complete a 554 for the town and county bill because you will be correcting a parcel that is incorrect on the assessment roll for the entire taxing year.
I think the key is to be consistent in what you do.  In my opinion, either they work it out for the school and then an apportionment for Town and County or conversely a refund for school and a 554 to correct the Town and County bill and then an omit for both next year on the new split parcel tax ID would be clean and consistent.
Good luck! This is a tough one.
Sarah Lippincott
Director of Real Property
Genesee County
15 Main Street
Batavia, NY 14020

subject: Re: Relevies for Villages, Schools, etc.
body:
Law reference time! I'll put the paragraph the language is in before the link.
Village taxes: sent to County within 15 days of end of village tax collection
(4.(a) NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov)School taxes: sent to County not later than November 15th (2.
NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov)Unpaid water/sewer: Town law 198 covers a lot of topics but Water (3(d)
NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov) specifically says that no later than November 1st the town clerk must file with the Supervisor a list of unpaid water accounts and the supervisor
shall then transmit such statements to "the board of supervisors of the county at its next regular meeting"
Alternatively what I do: just make your life easy and say everything needs to be submitted at the same time the Town budget is submitted to the County. Towns have until November 20th
to pass a budget (NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov), the Town Clerk must deliver within 5 day the final budget to the Town Supervisor (NYS
Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov), and the Town Supervisor must send the budget to the County within 10 days of receiving it from the Clerk (NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov). So - at the
end of the day, December 5th is the absolute latest a town can submit their budget to the County and the budget should include the amounts to be raised for any relevies to be added to tax bills.

Village taxes: sent to County within 15 days of end of village tax collection
(4.(a) NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov)School taxes: sent to County not later than November 15th (2.
NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov)Unpaid water/sewer: Town law 198 covers a lot of topics but Water (3(d)
NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov) specifically says that no later than November 1st the town clerk must file with the Supervisor a list of unpaid water accounts and the supervisor
shall then transmit such statements to "the board of supervisors of the county at its next regular meeting"
Alternatively what I do: just make your life easy and say everything needs to be submitted at the same time the Town budget is submitted to the County. Towns have until November 20th
to pass a budget (NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov), the Town Clerk must deliver within 5 day the final budget to the Town Supervisor (NYS
Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov), and the Town Supervisor must send the budget to the County within 10 days of receiving it from the Clerk (NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov). So - at the
end of the day, December 5th is the absolute latest a town can submit their budget to the County and the budget should include the amounts to be raised for any relevies to be added to tax bills.

subject: Re: Bill Processing Fees
body:
Some people who received this message don't often get email from corey.metz@oswegocountyny.gov.
Learn why this is important
We charge two separate fees: one for just the files and an additional fee if they want us to print the bills. The fee for files is then also different if it's for Schools/Villages
or Cities/Towns:
Item
Description
Price
Tax Billing Files (School Districts and Villages)
Production of files used in the creation of tax bills and updating of tax collection software (RPSv4 data files)
$0.55/per parcel
Tax Billing Files (Cities and Towns)
Production of files used in the creation of tax bills and updating of tax collection software (RPSv4 data files)
$0.20/per parcel
Tax Bill Printing
Seal form or bright white copy paper (depending on recipient). This charge is in addition to the fee for Tax Billing File production.
$0.20/per bill
Schedule of Fees
Back in 2023 I attempted to do a cost analysis based on labor, materials, and software costs. I've had pushback for charging the towns for files (even when they print their own bills)
because we just "push a button" to make them - and my justification has been that the only reason we're even able to provide those files is because we've spent an entire year maintaining and updating the database in order to be able to just "push a button"
to make them, so the file cost represents a per parcel cost for those efforts. And since the law says we have to provide them with the "tax roll" and not "convenient data files that can be imported easily into your tax collection software of choice" I think
it's only fair to charge back the cost to produce them.
Corey Metz

This has to do with STAR.  If the bill is greater than zero before the STAR benefit is subtracted from the total due, it will generate a zero-dollar bill.  You should not have zero-dollar
bills for any roll sections except roll section 1.

subject: Re: STRs
body:
$0.02 from someone who used to teach data collection--there are no statutory restrictions to data collection. Also, we used to remind assessors/data collectors that property classes
should reflect the use of the site. I remember having a similar discussion about 15 years ago with some folks up north (might have been Lewis County lol) and snowmobile garage/cabin rentals--whether they're 260s or something in the 400s, and the end
result was our usual advice "whatever you do, do it consistently so you know how to put the best value on it that you can." At the moment, a short term rental type house/cabin may not have the
best options, but I know plenty of assessors who do use 417 (cottages) or 418 (inn/lodge) as the property class, with the building inventory identified as a "converted residence" just like a converted house that became a bookstore or doctor's office
would be in their respective 4xx property classes. That said, it does make sense to bring it up to
someone, because the workarounds available to the assessment community don't identify short term rentals properly, they are lumped in with larger buildings like hotels/motels.
Also, ORPTS creates property classes, not NYS law. I would bring this to the VIT subcommittee of RPTAC. The issue is already on ORPTS's radar (I think it was discussed as a used-as code fairly recently, but I wasn't on VIT, it was only brought to me in the
context of RPS) so this new law may have already set things in motion (or they may be expecting the request from the community), and it's just a matter of updating RPS and the data collection manuals. Long story short: it's probably way easier than your supervisor
may think it will be!
I hope that helps and doesn't just come across as "um, actually" lol.
kk

Trish McLoughlin

Subject: Re: STRs
PUTNAM COUNTY NOTICE
THIS EMAIL IS FROM AN EXTERNAL SENDER! DO
NOT click links, DO NOT open attachments, DO NOT forward if you were not expecting this email or if it seems suspicious in any way! REMEMBER: NEVER provide your user ID or password to anyone for any reason!
The issue I forsee is potentially having to switch a property back and forth between a 200 class and a 400 class depending on the owner, sale and use.  A single family owner occupied home (210)
might sell to an investor (think estate sale) to be used as either a long term or short term rental (proposed 400 class) which might sell later to be used as an owner occupied home again (back to the 210).  While I can appreciate the intent and the overall
theory, I personally see this as more of a potent issue until and unless we can PROVE the rental/investment of a 200 class property.  Having a property owner register, comply with a questionaire or similar is likely to fail miserably.  Let's be honest: how
many properties do additions and other improvements without permits?  Do we really think an investor is going to voluntarily divulge that they are renting out a home?
Just my $.02

﻿To All: it's one thing to create a statewide registry of commercial or business residences ass noted in the email but as far as assessment records are concerned and the methods that
we use to arrive at residential values for one, two and three family homes,  theya have always been assessed by market sales (also classified as such as Homestead in Article 19 towns and in SCAR challenges as well) - this extra classification is unnecessary
for assessment purposes as a residential use would still be the same whether rented, short term leased or other combinations.  So I for one, will not be contributing to a potential argument that a residence could be some sort of commercial entity, as I could
see grievers, tax attorneys etc. arguing that an income approach is appropriate for a new class and could backfire and result in reducing its assessment value (as we often find with commercial properties using an income approach with exaggerated expenses,
vacancy, etc). As far as its effect on equalization, these sales, if necessary, can be argued as atypical ones that could actually reduce equalization ratios -not raise them - if sold solely for investment purposes and we could argue that they should be omitted
from Eq. and RAR calculations when they are reviewed with ORPTS each year. Taking into account other issues with these, compliances with permitting, zoning, safety, etc., that is another matter for building depts, planning and zoning boards, which compile
lists of these or wish to do so as here in Orangetown, but the overall market value is what I am concerned with. So, not a good idea at least as I see it for now.

subject: Re: STRs
body:
This is where legislation comes in. I agree that the income approach might be requested in terms of how to value an STR property and that is dangerous. So, we
should be out front asking for there to be legislation that says that STRs are valued through sales.
The simple fact is if STRs are driving up values and thus taxes in the residential market, we should find a way to pull them out of the residential market for
assessment purposes while ensuring that they are valued in a fair way that keeps their value on the roll. We should be always trying to drive down taxes for our true residents when we can by adding our voices and expertise to the legislative mix. Like it or
not we have a policy role in that we have an understanding of how this works that others do not.
I for one hope that ORPTS takes this up on a rule basis and that if so, we start pushing for legislation to ensure proper valuation methodology.
Victor L. Mallison

White Plains, NY 10601

﻿To All: it's one thing to create a statewide registry of commercial or business residences ass noted in the email but as far as assessment records are concerned and the methods that
we use to arrive at residential values for one, two and three family homes,  theya have always been assessed by market sales (also classified as such as Homestead in Article 19 towns and in SCAR challenges as well) - this extra classification is unnecessary
for assessment purposes as a residential use would still be the same whether rented, short term leased or other combinations.  So I for one, will not be contributing to a potential argument that a residence could be some sort of commercial entity, as I could
see grievers, tax attorneys etc. arguing that an income approach is appropriate for a new class and could backfire and result in reducing its assessment value (as we often find with commercial properties using an income approach with exaggerated expenses,
vacancy, etc). As far as its effect on equalization, these sales, if necessary, can be argued as atypical ones that could actually reduce equalization ratios -not raise them - if sold solely for investment purposes and we could argue that they should be omitted
from Eq. and RAR calculations when they are reviewed with ORPTS each year. Taking into account other issues with these, compliances with permitting, zoning, safety, etc., that is another matter for building depts, planning and zoning boards, which compile
lists of these or wish to do so as here in Orangetown, but the overall market value is what I am concerned with. So, not a good idea at least as I see it for now.

So, I have my county equalization and apportionment spreadsheet basically done, just waiting until our public hearing and adoption of the county's budget to get the levy. SCAR decisions are done for this year,
so, barring any corrections of error, or the off-chance that an Article 7 that is hanging out there fiiinally settles, I am good to go. Or so I thought.

Meghan.

body:
In our Towns a County engineer signs off on the demolitions to make sure that the buildings are facing eminent collapse and also are a danger to the public.
If the building is isolated and not a danger to the public then we do not sign off on the demo.  If the municipality proceeds to demolish these then we do not guarantee that we will make the relevied demolition cost whole.
The City of Albany has their own process.  We guarantee any and all costs associate with the demolition.

This is a little different, but Jefferson County recently passed a resolution that allows the county Code Enforcement office to step in extreme cases when a parcel becomes a danger to the public.  In this process, I believe the County will
pay for what needs to be done to make the property safe, then bill the property owner.  I've been asked about the process of relevying that bill to the tax bill if the property owner doesn't pay it.
Do any of your counties have a similar process?  In the past here, normally towns and villages have been involved in these types of actions.
Have a wonderful week,
Alex

subject: RPTL §480-a Penalties – County Practices
body:
Hi everyone,
I am seeking input on how other counties handle the assessment and administration of penalties under RPTL §480-a.
A property owner in my county has indicated that they no longer wish to continue with their approved forest management plan. I provided an estimate of the penalties that could apply if the exemption is not renewed for the upcoming roll year and the owner
fails to comply with the required work schedule under the agreement (with the next scheduled treatment not until 2030). The owner has since stated that DEC advised him that the imposition of penalties is ultimately determined at the county level. He is requesting
a reduced penalty and formal written documentation outlining the amount, and our county has very limited prior guidance or precedent on this issue.
I am trying to determine whether counties typically treat the penalty as strictly statutory with no discretion, or whether any discretion is exercised in practice, as well as how this is formally documented and communicated to the property owner. I have
not been able to locate any prior examples in our county, so any insight into how your county handles this situation would be greatly appreciated.
Thank you!
Victoria Blancato
Director, Real Property Tax Services
Wyoming County
143 North Main Street, Warsaw, NY 14569
Phone: (585) 786-8828 | Email: vblancato@wyomingcountyny.gov
https://www.wyomingcountyny.gov/

subject: Re: RPTL §480-a Penalties – County Practices
body:
The DEC must determine that there was a violation of the forestry plan before any penalties can be assessed.  They would send a notice to the county treasurer which would trigger
penalties.  Nothing can be done by the county until a notice of violation has been received.
Also, as far as I know the penalty is not negotiable.  The only way to make a change to it is if there was a miscalculation.  I do not calculate the penalties, the finance department
does.  I only add them to the roll if they don't get paid in time for County/Town bills.
Cathy Weisse
Director of Real Property Tax Services
Dutchess County Real Property Tax Service Agency
22 Market Street
Poughkeepsie, NY  12601

Subject: (EXTERNAL) RPTL §480-a Penalties - County Practices
CAUTION:  unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe.
Hi everyone,
I am seeking input on how other counties handle the assessment and administration of penalties under RPTL §480-a.
A property owner in my county has indicated that they no longer wish to continue with their approved forest management plan. I provided an estimate of the penalties that could apply if the exemption is not renewed for the upcoming roll year and the owner
fails to comply with the required work schedule under the agreement (with the next scheduled treatment not until 2030). The owner has since stated that DEC advised him that the imposition of penalties is ultimately determined at the county level. He is requesting
a reduced penalty and formal written documentation outlining the amount, and our county has very limited prior guidance or precedent on this issue.
I am trying to determine whether counties typically treat the penalty as strictly statutory with no discretion, or whether any discretion is exercised in practice, as well as how this is formally documented and communicated to the property owner. I have
not been able to locate any prior examples in our county, so any insight into how your county handles this situation would be greatly appreciated.
Thank you!
Victoria Blancato
Director, Real Property Tax Services
Wyoming County
143 North Main Street, Warsaw, NY 14569
Phone: (585) 786-8828 | Email: vblancato@wyomingcountyny.gov
https://www.wyomingcountyny.gov/

subject: Can a town levy a penalty on a tax bill
body:
One of my towns is asking for guidance: They want to put in a new refuse law, which, once adopted, would authorize the issuance of fines to homeowners who violate its provisions. If a homeowner fails to pay
an issued fine, the Town would like to explore the option of levying the unpaid fine onto the homeowner's tax bill as a means of enforcement and collection.
Can they do that? I thought that they can charge a tax all they want and if it does not get paid then it gets relevied and goes onto the next County bill, and that was that. But putting a fine for lack of
payment onto the town tax bill? Not sure about that one.
And yes, they need to check with their municipal attorney, but their muni attorney is leaving, and they want an answer before their next meeting on Wednesday. And, also yes, I can tell them to wait until they
get a new muni attorney and then ask them, but I wanted to know if what they are asking is completely reasonable, or completely unreasonable.
Paul Wiley
Director
Orange County Office of Real Property
255 Main St
Goshen, NY 10924

body:
Deeds and 5217's come through every week from the CC by town.  We have a digital deed folder and a digital 5217 folder.  We print the 5217's for scanning
to the State.  We keep those in paper form for about a month, and then they go in the garbage.  Our CC, via IQS, has all of the deeds, accessible by their website, as well.  All of our property cards/notes were digitized last year by way of help from a summer
intern and our Records Dept jumped in and helped.  Now we have Schneider/Beacon, so we just keep adding 'Notes' on properties as things change.  Very few cabinets in our office!

Re: RPTL §480-a Penalties – County Practices
body:
In Otsego County we have in the past reached out to each municipality (county, school, town, and village) and asked them if they wanted to waive the penalties, interest, and fines - because they are definitely excessive, but they are set by the 480a law.
But once we got a resolution from every municipality waiving all the fees, interest, and penalties, we were able to accept just the base amount.
Please note my new email address: rufflesa@otsegocountyny.gov
Allen Ruffles

Sent: Monday, December 15, 2025 10:01:51 AM
Subject: RPTL §480-a Penalties - County Practices
Hi everyone, I am seeking input on how other counties handle the assessment and administration of penalties under RPTL §480-a. A property owner in my county has indicated that they no longer wish to continue with their approved forest management
Hi everyone,
I am seeking input on how other counties handle the assessment and administration of penalties under RPTL §480-a.
A property owner in my county has indicated that they no longer wish to continue with their approved forest management plan. I provided an estimate of the penalties that could apply if the exemption is not renewed for the upcoming roll year and the owner
fails to comply with the required work schedule under the agreement (with the next scheduled treatment not until 2030). The owner has since stated that DEC advised him that the imposition of penalties is ultimately determined at the county level. He is requesting
a reduced penalty and formal written documentation outlining the amount, and our county has very limited prior guidance or precedent on this issue.
I am trying to determine whether counties typically treat the penalty as strictly statutory with no discretion, or whether any discretion is exercised in practice, as well as how this is formally documented and communicated to the property owner. I have
not been able to locate any prior examples in our county, so any insight into how your county handles this situation would be greatly appreciated.
Thank you!
Victoria Blancato
Director, Real Property Tax Services
Wyoming County

subject: Re: PILOT Payments
body:
Our IDA goes after them for the payments, and if they're not made, the PILOT is revoked, effective the date of the missed payment, and we end up putting the taxes on as omitted taxes the next year. We had one this year that was revoked effective back to final
roll, but paperwork didn't come through until after school bills. We don't do CoE increases without the owner's signature, so we reached out to them (and the IDA reached out) asking if they wanted the CoE or if they wanted us to add it to the next school bill,
and we never heard back, so...double bill for next year it is.

subject: Re: Technical Question on Bills going to Collectors/Receivers
body:
The tax warrant just authorizes the collector(s) to enforce collection of taxes contained in the tax roll. RPTL 922 (NYS
Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov) states:
§ 922. Statement of taxes to be mailed. 1. (a) Upon receipt of the tax
roll and warrant, the collecting officer shall mail or, subject to the
provisions of section one hundred four of this chapter, transmit
electronically to each owner of real property at the tax billing address
listed thereon a statement showing the amount of taxes due on the
property.
Nothing prevents the bills from being printed prior to receipt of the warrant, they just shouldn't be mailed until they have a Warrant to collect.
Corey Metz

subject: Re: Bill Processing Fees
body:
In Essex County, we charge Towns, Schools and Villages $0.60/parcel. In addition to that, we charge for each binder used and any additional copies they may request.
For the towns, that $0.60/parcel covers tax roll, tentative assessment roll and final assessment roll. We charge another $0.60 per change of assessment notice printed (we mail them for the towns). Towns are also charged for each binder used for all of their
rolls.
I am bringing forward a request to increase these charges this month.

subject: Updated Veteran Disabled Exemption
body:
Are you all getting inundated with questions about the update to the disabled vet exemption as well?
https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S1183
From what I'm seeing it would only apply to the value added by installing things like ramps, etc. It's also opt-in and has other requirements as well.
"GOVERNMENT AND HAS APPLIED SUCH ASSISTANCE  TOWARD  THE  ACQUISITION  OR
MODIFICATION OF A SUITABLE HOUSING UNIT WITH SPECIAL FEATURES OR MOVABLE
FACILITIES  MADE NECESSARY BY THE NATURE OF THE VETERANS' DISABILITY AND
THE  NECESSARY  LAW  THEREFOR  SHALL  BE  FULLY EXEMPT FROM TAXATION AND
SPECIAL DISTRICT CHARGES, ASSESSMENTS AND  SPECIAL  AD  VALOREM  LEVIES,
PROVIDED THAT SUCH VETERAN MEETS ALL OTHER REQUIREMENTS OF THIS SECTION.
§ 2. This act shall take effect immediately and shall apply to assess-
ment rolls prepared on and after January 2, 2026."
Are you reading it the same? I have vets thinking that it will give them 100% tax free status.
--------------------------------------------------------------------

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) Re: [EXTERNAL] Updated Veteran Disabled Exemption
body:
Folks,
The following was forwarded to me from one of my assessors:
Good morning --
I hope that this message finds you safe and well.
On December 19, S.1183 -- a bill regarding the ability of certain Veterans in New York State to receive a total exemption on their property taxes -- was signed into law. Since then, our Department has received many questions regarding this
legislation and its impact, as there is understandably some confusion about these matters.
The summary of this bill states: "Amend the real property tax law by adding a new subdivision 3-a which would mandate an exemption from all taxes imposed upon disabled veterans and his or her spouse, with a one hundred percent service
connected disability."
Overall, the perception is that this newly enacted law provides a total property tax exemption for all Veterans with a 100% disability compensation rating from the VA.
However, this perception -- while it matches a lot of the public messaging surrounding this bill -- does not match the reality of what this bill actually says.
First, this law establishes a local option, not a statewide mandate. Each locality gets to decide for themselves whether they wish to enact a local law or other equivalent measure providing the opportunity for certain Veterans to receive
a total property tax exemption.
Secondly, the bill does not provide a total exemption for all Veterans with a 100% disability compensation rating.
The language of the legislation requires that a Veteran must have a
qualifying condition under NYS Veterans' Services Law defined as Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), or experiencing Military Sexual Trauma (MST)
or a discharged LGBT Veteran with an other than dishonorable or bad conduct discharge
and a 100% rating with a permanent and total designation from the VA,
and a Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability (TDIU) designation from the VA,
and also qualify for the VA's specially adapted housing grant.
Unless a Veteran meets all of these required criteria, they will not qualify for the total exemption even if they live in a community whose local government adopted this exemption.
Some people have contacted me since December 19 stating that the drafters of the bill must not have intended for the bill to have so many requirements for a Veteran to qualify for the total exemption. Perhaps this is true. We do not know.
Regardless of the intent of the legislature, the role of a government's executive branch is to carry out the laws as written. The language here requires plainly that a Veteran meet all four criteria described above to qualify for the total exemption. The executive
branch is therefore bound by this language.
What happens next? Given the gap between what the new law actually says and what the individuals advocating for the law's enactment apparently believed it to say, the probable next step would be a chapter amendment attempting to bridge
this gap. This is a process that we saw function successfully earlier this year with the legislation to expand the pool of Veterans who can receive New York State's Veterans Tuition Award, where all sides came together to agree upon the best language to amend
New York State's Education Law in a manner that achieved this objective.
Should the legislature pursue a chapter amendment, we cannot predict what this chapter amendment will ultimately say, nor do we know the pace at which this process will proceed. Once we know any concrete information on these topics, we
will certainly share it with you.
Please feel free to let me know if you have any questions regarding this legislation and its impacts, and I will answer them gladly to the best of my ability. Of course, as you can already see, some questions might not be answerable at
this stage in the process, and in such situations I will let you know this as well.
Thank you greatly, as always, for the advocacy that you provide to Veterans, Service Members, and Military Families every day.
Respectfully,
Benjamin P. Pomerance
Deputy Counsel
Pronouns: He/Him
New York State Department of Veterans' Services
2 Empire State Plaza, 17th Floor, Albany, NY 12223
Michael McGuire, IAO, CCD
Director
Albany County Real Property Tax Service Agency
112 State Street, Room 1103, Albany, NY 12207

body:
Hello All,
Please note that the 2026 winter conference will be held
March 16 - March 18, 2026
at the Hotel Trilogy.  NYSAC changed the date of their conference so to continue to coincide with that conference, I have arranged with Hotel Trilogy for the new March dates.
Make sure to call the hotel and book your room no later than February 21, 2026!  No rooms will be guaranteed after that date.
Once again, we are utilizing electronic registration forms; the link or QR code are below.  Non-Directors will still need to use the attached PDF and should not fill out the online registration form.  I have attached registration forms
for those that need them for internal purposes.
NYSACDRPTS 2026 Winter Legislative Conference
Directors should use this link or QR Code to register online for the conference: Non-Directors will need to complete that attached 2025 Winter Conference Non-Director Registration Form.
2026 Winter Legislative Conference Registration
We have a block of 35 rooms reserved for the 16th through 18th, with 15 being held for the 15th for anyone coming in on Sunday.  The room rate is $117 per night.  You can call the Hotel Trilogy at (518) 869-9100 to make your room reservation.
The room block will be held until February 21st.  Any reservations made after the 21st are not guaranteed and will only be filled if there is availability.  Please call to reserve your room as soon as possible.
I hope to get a tentative schedule out next month.
Feel free to contact me with any questions that you may have.  Happy New Year!!!
Thank you,

subject: Question: mailing deadline for bills
body:
Question--for those of you who mail the county/town bills for your towns, what's your "goal" date? Are you done mailing before Christmas? Before the new year? Before...idk, the 5th?
We got slammed with the snowstorm Tuesday so the office was shut down one day, then less than half staff NYE because folks hadn't been able to dig out, so we missed our goal of getting all of our (over 100k, since we pull escrows and utilities) bills in the
mail by Wednesday and now one of my receivers is raising a ruckus that she, the town supervisor, and board are getting calls after calls because people haven't gotten their tax bill yet (they've been online since Monday). I'm trying to gauge where that sits
in terms of level of concern--like, on a scale of "OMG, most places are barely done printing right now, chill" to "You're right, of course you should have had that paper in your hands before the 31st, we will do better."
Thanks,
Kate
Kathleen Kearney, Director
Real Property Tax Services
Onondaga County

Syracuse, New York 13202

subject: Re: Question: mailing deadline for bills
body:
We don't mail on behalf of the towns, but we do print them all and the collector's pick them up from us. Every year they insist they need them before Christmas because they need to get them in the mail so everyone has their bills before the 1st and
we always try and accommodate, but it's always nice to remind them that:
RPTL 922 says "Upon receipt of the tax roll and warrant, the collecting officer shall mail [...] to each owner of real property at the tax billing address listed thereon a statement showing the amount of taxes
due on the property" and since the Warrant can be as late as December 31st the law was never intended to say taxpayers needed a tax bill in their hands on or before January 1st
You don't even need a tax bill in order to pay the taxes (it's just a friendly reminder)
Failure to even mail a bill doesn't affect the validity of taxes
We can always go back an follow the letter of the law (see #1) and just send them a tax roll and some blank tax bills and they can hand print them and put them in the mail like the good ol' days before computers
(ignore the fact I am too young to remember a time in which this would have been done any other way)

Subject: Re: Question: mailing deadline for bills
This message originated from outside of the organization.
We don't mail on behalf of the towns, but we do print them all and the collector's pick them up from us. Every year they insist they need them before Christmas because they need to get them in the mail so everyone has their bills before the 1st and
we always try and accommodate, but it's always nice to remind them that:
RPTL 922 says "Upon receipt of the tax roll and warrant, the collecting officer shall mail [...] to each owner of real property at the tax billing address listed thereon a statement showing the amount of taxes
due on the property" and since the Warrant can be as late as December 31st the law was never intended to say taxpayers needed a tax bill in their hands on or before January 1st
You don't even need a tax bill in order to pay the taxes (it's just a friendly reminder)
Failure to even mail a bill doesn't affect the validity of taxes
We can always go back an follow the letter of the law (see #1) and just send them a tax roll and some blank tax bills and they can hand print them and put them in the mail like the good ol' days before computers
(ignore the fact I am too young to remember a time in which this would have been done any other way)

Legislative Updates: Governor signs bill to allow for a disability exemption for
veterans with a 100 percent disability rating
Governor Hochul has signed a bill to allow for a disability exemption for veterans with a 100 percent disability rating -
please read carefully!
The Governor has signed bill
S.01183 / A.00074, which establishes a new real property tax exemption related to veterans with service-connected disabilities.
Please read the following carefully, as the scope of this legislation is very specific and subject to local adoption.
The exemption is not automatic. Each taxing jurisdiction must adopt a local law or equivalent measure to offer this exemption. If a taxing jurisdiction does not adopt it, the exemption does
not apply within that jurisdiction.
This is NOT a blanket exemption for all veterans with a 100% disability rating.
Despite public perception, the law does
not provide a total exemption for all veterans receiving a 100% disability compensation rating from the VA.
To qualify, a veteran must meet
all the following criteria:
·
Have a qualifying condition under NYS Veterans' Services Law, defined as:
o
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD),
or
o
Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI),
or
o
Military Sexual Trauma (MST),
or
o
Be a discharged LGBT Veteran with an other-than-dishonorable or bad conduct discharge;
and
·
Have a
100% disability rating with a
Permanent and Total designation from the VA;
and
·
Have a
Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability (TDIU) designation from the VA;
and
·
Qualify for the VA's
specially adapted housing grant.
Unless
all these statutory requirements are met, the veteran is
not eligible for the total exemption even if the taxing jurisdiction has adopted the local option.
Given the likelihood of questions from taxpayers and local officials, members are encouraged to review the statute carefully and coordinate with their
municipal attorneys before any local action is taken.
The Association expects that the bill sponsors may request a chapter amendment to address concerns or clarify intent, however, there is no indication
if, when, or how long that process may take. The Association will continue to monitor the legislation and provide updates as information becomes available.
Click here to review the legislation -

Legislative Updates: Governor signs bill to allow for a disability exemption for veterans with a 100 percent disability rating
Governor Hochul has signed a bill to allow for a disability exemption for veterans with a 100 percent disability rating - please read carefully!
The Governor has signed bill S.01183 / A.00074, which establishes a new real property tax exemption related to veterans with service-connected disabilities. Please read the following carefully, as the scope of this legislation is very specific and subject to local adoption.
The exemption is not automatic. Each taxing jurisdiction must adopt a local law or equivalent measure to offer this exemption. If a taxing jurisdiction does not adopt it, the exemption does not apply within that jurisdiction.
This is NOT a blanket exemption for all veterans with a 100% disability rating. Despite public perception, the law does not provide a total exemption for all veterans receiving a 100% disability compensation rating from the VA.
To qualify, a veteran must meet all the following criteria:
Have a qualifying condition under NYS Veterans' Services Law, defined as:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), or
Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), or
Military Sexual Trauma (MST), or
Be a discharged LGBT Veteran with an other-than-dishonorable or bad conduct discharge; and
Have a 100% disability rating with a Permanent and Total designation from the VA; and
Have a Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability (TDIU) designation from the VA; and
Qualify for the VA's specially adapted housing grant.
Unless all these statutory requirements are met, the veteran is not eligible for the total exemption even if the taxing jurisdiction has adopted the local option.
Given the likelihood of questions from taxpayers and local officials, members are encouraged to review the statute carefully and coordinate with their municipal attorneys before any local action is taken.
The Association expects that the bill sponsors may request a chapter amendment to address concerns or clarify intent, however, there is no indication if, when, or how long that process may take. The Association will continue to monitor the legislation and provide updates as information becomes available.
Click here to review the legislation - https://nyassembly.gov/leg/?default_fld=%0D%0A&leg_video=&bn=A074&term=2025&Summary=Y&Text=Y
Sincerely,
Maggie Alix
Scott J. Schedler, IAO

subject: NY Gen Bus Law 518 - credit card fees
body:
Our new credit card readers through Hamer and M&T Bank do not provide the final amounts to be paid when taxes are paid in person via credit.  Instead, the card reader/machine provides the taxes being paid and the receipt we provide from
our tax collection software is supposed to list the taxes plus credit card fee amount.  Under NY Gen Bus Law § 518, the card reader should show the final amount being paid, including fees.  We have a little bit of a dispute going on internally regarding whether
the reader has to supply the final figure, or can signage and a statement supply the percentage to be added (something that is prohibited under GBL 518, but some people are saying that since we are a County the law is inapplicable).  Any experience or guidance
would be greatly appreciated.  Thanks!

This message originated from outside of the organization.
We don't mail on behalf of the towns, but we do print them all and the collector's pick them up from us. Every year they insist they need them before Christmas because they need to get them in the mail so everyone has their bills before the 1st and
we always try and accommodate, but it's always nice to remind them that:
RPTL 922 says "Upon receipt of the tax roll and warrant, the collecting officer shall mail [...] to each owner of real property at the tax billing address listed thereon a statement showing the amount of taxes
due on the property" and since the Warrant can be as late as December 31st the law was never intended to say taxpayers needed a tax bill in their hands on or before January 1st
You don't even need a tax bill in order to pay the taxes (it's just a friendly reminder)
Failure to even mail a bill doesn't affect the validity of taxes
We can always go back an follow the letter of the law (see #1) and just send them a tax roll and some blank tax bills and they can hand print them and put them in the mail like the good ol' days before computers
(ignore the fact I am too young to remember a time in which this would have been done any other way)
Corey Metz

Question--for those of you who mail the county/town bills for your towns, what's your "goal" date? Are you done mailing before Christmas? Before the new year? Before...idk, the 5th?
We got slammed with the snowstorm Tuesday so the office was shut down one day, then less than half staff NYE because folks hadn't been able to dig out, so we missed our goal of getting all of our (over 100k, since we pull escrows and utilities) bills in the
mail by Wednesday and now one of my receivers is raising a ruckus that she, the town supervisor, and board are getting calls after calls because people haven't gotten their tax bill yet (they've been online since Monday). I'm trying to gauge where that sits
in terms of level of concern--like, on a scale of "OMG, most places are barely done printing right now, chill" to "You're right, of course you should have had that paper in your hands before the 31st, we will do better."

Hello
There is a tax payer accusing the assessor of potentially breaking RPTL 305(2).
The town has an eq. rate of 70.  The subdivision this person lives in has been developed since the last town-wide revaluation.  The property owner is stating that the
assessor is breaking the law because her fair market value exceeds the actual fair market value.  This entire subdivision is potentially over valued because they are all newly built homes with next to no resales since the original  purchase.
The assessor and I have explained at length the process she needs to follow to protest her assessment.  She just doesn't want to listen and insists that the AV be reduced
NOW without trying or wanting to understand this isn't possible at this time.  She thinks that if she completes the grievance form now it should be reviewed and changed now.  I have suggested an appraisal be completed and the assessor review it for a possible
reduction to the 26 roll.
Who has any suggestions to better explain and help this property owner understand what she needs to do going forward?

Have a great evening

subject: Special District Changes after Final Roll
body:
Good afternoon,
We got changes in October to special districts in one of our towns. It was after we'd locked our roll for editing so we could work on T/C bills, and we assumed it was intended for the 2026 roll year, but I just got an email that the intent was for corrections
to the 2025 roll and now I'm questioning whether my assumption was silly and the only changes we really restrict should be assessed value changes? Is it common practice to update special districts right before T/C bills? (in addition to move tax charges, of
course)
Thanks y'all
Kate
Kathleen Kearney, Director
Real Property Tax Services
Onondaga County
421 Montgomery St, 15th Floor
Syracuse, New York 13202
www.ongov.net/RPTS
P: (315) 435-2426

subject: Re: Special District Changes after Final Roll
body:
Hi Kate,
Special Districts are a beast on their own!!  If all the steps were followed per statute to create the special district (or to change it), then yes, it can be done prior to taxes being levied.  Since the town
files would have been frozen at that point, it would fall on the county to update.  At least that's how we do it in Lewis County.
We had a single town fire district separated into three different districts after final roll was completed and we used the three new districts on the county/town bill that year.

We don't mail on behalf of the towns, but we do print them all and the collector's pick them up from us. Every year they insist they need them before Christmas because they need
to get them in the mail so everyone has their bills before the 1st and we always try and accommodate, but it's always nice to remind them that:
RPTL 922 says "Upon receipt of the tax roll and warrant, the collecting officer shall mail [...] to each owner of real property at the tax billing address listed thereon a statement showing the amount of taxes
due on the property" and since the Warrant can be as late as December 31st the law was never intended to say taxpayers needed a tax bill in their hands on or before January 1st
You don't even need a tax bill in order to pay the taxes (it's just a friendly reminder)
Failure to even mail a bill doesn't affect the validity of taxes
We can always go back an follow the letter of the law (see #1) and just send them a tax roll and some blank tax bills and they can hand print them and put them in the mail like the good ol' days before computers
(ignore the fact I am too young to remember a time in which this would have been done any other way)
Corey Metz

Question--for those of you who mail the county/town bills for your towns, what's your "goal" date? Are you done mailing before Christmas? Before the new year? Before...idk, the 5th?
We got slammed with the snowstorm Tuesday so the office was shut down one day, then less than half staff NYE because folks hadn't been able to dig out, so we missed our goal of getting all of
our (over 100k, since we pull escrows and utilities) bills in the mail by Wednesday and now one of my receivers is raising a ruckus that she, the town supervisor, and board are getting calls after calls because people haven't gotten their tax bill yet (they've
been online since Monday). I'm trying to gauge where that sits in terms of level of concern--like, on a scale of "OMG, most places are barely done printing right now, chill" to "You're right, of course you should have had that paper in your hands before the

subject: Re: Guidance Needed on Handling Subdivision Not Reflected on 2025 Assessment Roll
body:
Hi everyone,
I wanted to follow up on a situation I raised earlier regarding a parcel where a portion was conveyed in 2024 but was not reflected on the tax map or  assessment roll/RPS until 2026. Several of you suggested that an apportionment of the
tax bills may be the best way to address this.
Before proceeding, I wanted to clarify a few points. Since the newly created parcel does not formally exist on the roll until 2026, is an apportionment still possible for the prior tax years? If so, how would that typically be processed
on the tax collectors' end?
Thank you!
Victoria Blancato
Director, Real Property Tax Services
Wyoming County
143 North Main Street, Warsaw, NY 14569
Phone: (585) 786-8828 | Email: vblancato@wyomingcountyny.gov
https://www.wyomingcountyny.gov/
From: Real Property Tax Directors <RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US>
On Behalf Of Candy Akin
Sent: Wednesday, November 19, 2025 3:20 PM
To: RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US
Subject: Re: Guidance Needed on Handling Subdivision Not Reflected on 2025 Assessment Roll
Tori,
You would want to do a tax apportionment.  The assessor will need to put an apportioned value on each parcel and then, depending on how your county handles it, the tax bill can be split.  Not sure if you
do that or if your tax collectors handle it.
In the Members section of our website, there are some samples of form and worksheets to accomplish this.
Candy Akin, CCD
Real Property Tax Director
2025-2026 President, NYSACDRPTS
O: 315-376-5336
M: 315-907-2032
candyakin@lewiscounty.ny.gov
7660 North State St. | Lowville, NY 13367
From: Real Property Tax Directors <RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US>
On Behalf Of Victoria Blancato
Sent: Wednesday, November 19, 2025 2:30 PM
To: RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US
Subject: Guidance Needed on Handling Subdivision Not Reflected on 2025 Assessment Roll
Hi everyone,
We have a property where a portion of vacant land was sold in September 2024. Due to an error with the deed/survey map, the subdivision was not processed in our system in time for the taxable status date, so the parcel was not split on
the 2025 assessment roll. As a result:
The new owner of the subdivided portion has not received a school tax bill.The previous owner of the original parcel is being taxed on the entire acreage.
I'm looking for guidance on the best way to handle this. My current thinking is to file an RP-556 to refund the original owner for the school taxes. At this point, I would prefer not to make any changes to the roll before the town/county
bills so I would also do a correction afterward for original owner to the town/county tax roll. Would the proper approach then be to treat the amount the new owner should have paid as omits next year?
Thank you!
Victoria Blancato
Director, Real Property Tax Services
Wyoming County
143 North Main Street, Warsaw, NY 14569
Phone: (585) 786-8828 | Email: vblancato@wyomingcountyny.gov
https://www.wyomingcountyny.gov/

We would also do the same--A BAR or SCAR decision denying the request to lower assessments/change data isn't the same as telling the assessor they can't change it, it's just telling the taxpayer "we don't think there's enough information for us to override the
assessment/data." If the assessor were to re-review and say "actually, you were right" and then file the 554/556, we would do the correction.

I had a school district reach out after an Article 7 was received that was signed on January 7th 2026 reducing the 2025 Assessment creating a refund.  Their question was that since the original school tax bill had been paid in
September, should a 1099 be issued from the district since they will most likely be claiming or have claimed the higher original amount as a reduction on their taxes in 2025? Has anyone ever heard of a 1099 being sent after an Article 7 decision is issued?
Thanks,
Sarah Lippincott
Director of Real Property
Genesee County
15 Main Street
Batavia, NY 14020

subject: Re: 1099 - Article 7
body:
I have not heard of such a thing. It would be interesting as the payments are in two different tax years, the school tax payment and the refund. This will be a 1099 impacting the individuals
taxes by April 2027.
Vic

subject: senior exemption
body:
Good morning,
Is anyone else passing the senior exemption for this year? If so how have you interpreted the % issue - we decided to increase both the income limits and the % to 65% - then decrease the % accordingly  down to 35%
There has been concerns from the assessors that the lowest % in this scenario should be 20% which makes no sense to me at all - why increase the top % and not level down accordingly -
Thoughts?
anna

subject: Re: [ EXTERNAL ]  senior exemption
body:
We are moving forward just proposing adding the additional % increase, so anyone who has the exemption at 5% to 45% would not be affected at all, and then anyone with the 50% exemption would shift if their income is low enough. I did the same report--what
is the "max" effect on county revenue (assuming everyone who gets 50% now were to get 65%) and our County Executive reviewed it. I'm not sure what the towns are doing yet, we haven't met to discuss it, but I think most were not going to be pushing for 2026
roll changes.

subject: PILOT payment tracking
body:
Hi all - do you (or someone you know) track PILOT payments for your county? Our Treasurer's office is trying to find a good way to be able to pull up some manner of report or file to show who pays what in
PILOTs in a more robust way than just "they send us checks and we cash them". So if you have an example you could share with me, or any advice, it would be greatly appreciated!
Corey Metz
(She/her/hers)
Director | REAL
PROPERTY TAX SERVICES

Subject: [EXTERNAL] Re: (EXTERNAL) transfer of exempt property to non exempt owner
520 allows the assessor to reassess the property as of the date of transfer. It was set up that way so that things like churches can get properly assessed when they sell to a non-exempt owner. The assessor never looks at those assessments until they need to.
Here's the portion of 520 that talks about it:
2.  If  within the fiscal year during which a transfer of title occurs
or within the next succeeding fiscal year, an assessor is made aware  of
the  fact  that  title  to  real  property  receiving a total or partial
exemption from taxation has been transferred to a person, corporation or
association not otherwise entitled to an exemption from taxation, he  or
she   shall forthwith assess such property at its value as of the date of
transfer, shall, where appropriate for purposes of article  eighteen  or
nineteen  of this chapter, reclassify the property, and shall notify the
new owner of the assessment and of the right of that owner to  a  review
of  the  assessment and reclassification, if appropriate, as provided by
title three of article five of this chapter.
Whenever we get these, we always reach out to the assessor to see if they want to reassess it before we do the omitted.

subject: Re: transfer of exempt property to non-exempt owner
body:
Hi, Paul -
When a R/S 8 parcel will be going to R/S 1 on the next tax roll due to a sale and there is a change of use, the assessor may complete the attached form with the new assessment as of the date of
sale and the omitted tax will be based on that new number (ex - building that had been used as a church, new owner using as single family).
Whenever I see these sales, I reach out to the assessor to see if this is the case so they can return this form to me with the new assessed value (as of the date of transfer) prior to when I calculate
the omitted taxes.
Have a nice afternoon,
Meghan.

To: RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US <RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US>
Subject: [EXTERNAL] Re: (EXTERNAL) transfer of exempt property to non exempt owner
520 allows the assessor to reassess the property as of the date of transfer. It was set up that way so that things like churches can get properly assessed when they sell to a non-exempt owner. The assessor
never looks at those assessments until they need to.
Here's the portion of 520 that talks about it:
2.  If  within the fiscal year during which a transfer of title occurs
or within the next succeeding fiscal year, an assessor is made aware  of
the  fact  that  title  to  real  property  receiving a total or partial
exemption from taxation has been transferred to a person, corporation or
association not otherwise entitled to an exemption from taxation, he  or
she
shall forthwith assess such property at its value as of the date of
transfer, shall, where appropriate for purposes of article  eighteen  or
nineteen  of this chapter, reclassify the property, and shall notify the
new owner of the assessment and of the right of that owner to  a  review
of  the  assessment and reclassification, if appropriate, as provided by
title three of article five of this chapter.
Whenever we get these, we always reach out to the assessor to see if they want to reassess it before we do the omitted.

subject: Article 7
body:
Good morning, all -
So, I have my county equalization and apportionment spreadsheet basically done, just waiting until our public hearing and adoption of the county's budget to get the levy. SCAR decisions are done for this year,
so, barring any corrections of error, or the off-chance that an Article 7 that is hanging out there fiiinally settles, I am good to go. Or so I thought.
Just heard from one of my town assessors that an Article 7 case in her town DID just settle. I asked her to send me a copy. She did, but it isn't signed - not by the petitioner, the assessor, and, most significantly,
not the judge.
So, I am trying to track down an official signed order.
It got me to thinking though... Do you have a cut-off date that you will make changes to your file for Article 7 or SCAR decisions when working on town & county processing? It would be great to get the correct
amount on the town and county tax bill, but changes alter the town and county rates, my apportionment spreadsheet, etc, so there I have to draw the line at some point.
Anyway, let me know if you have a cut-off date, or if it varies year-to-year.
Thanks so much,
Meghan.

520 allows the assessor to reassess the property as of the date of transfer. It was set up that way so that things like churches can get properly assessed when they sell to a non-exempt owner. The assessor
never looks at those assessments until they need to.
Here's the portion of 520 that talks about it:
2.  If  within the fiscal year during which a transfer of title occurs
or within the next succeeding fiscal year, an assessor is made aware  of
the  fact  that  title  to  real  property  receiving a total or partial
exemption from taxation has been transferred to a person, corporation or
association not otherwise entitled to an exemption from taxation, he  or
she
shall forthwith assess such property at its value as of the date of
transfer, shall, where appropriate for purposes of article  eighteen  or
nineteen  of this chapter, reclassify the property, and shall notify the
new owner of the assessment and of the right of that owner to  a  review
of  the  assessment and reclassification, if appropriate, as provided by
title three of article five of this chapter.
Whenever we get these, we always reach out to the assessor to see if they want to reassess it before we do the omitted.

I would like to look at a system of emailing tax bills to property owners instead of mailing (this would be optional), the mailing costs continue to go up, and the delivery satisfaction is going down.  Add

OK, I know having complaints of "late" bills on January 5th was ridiculous. But we're still getting many calls daily from taxpayers who haven't gotten their bills. So are most of our receivers. And receivers
are noticing a huge drop in mailed-in payments--like, 30% of what they'd see by now in previous years (and not a huge increase in online payments).
All of our bills were sent out Dec 29th through Jan 2nd . One of the towns that mails their own has popped into the discussion that she's also had similar complaints, and the USPS has told
taxpayers it can take 2-3 weeks for mail to get to her snowbirds who got mail in FL. Has anyone else had significant issues like this?

subject: Re: Bulk Mail issues

We had to release a public statement about it last week, that folks can print and pay their bills online if they want--we were still getting 20+ calls a day here about missing tax bills. Mostly snowbirds by now, but still.

subject: Re: PILOT
body:
If we have a situation where we're ABLE to correct a tax bill and add the amount to that year, we will ask the IDA to reach out to the owner and see what they'd rather do. We had one PILOT that was rescinded the first week of September. We let them know that
we could add the school taxes to this year, since the bills had just gone out, and they could pay it now, OR we'd do it as omitted taxes next year. They never responded, so it'll be omitted taxes. But we only will do that if the owner signs the change request.
I think that's just our policy though.

subject: Office Structure Question
body:
Some people who received this message don't often get email from 000000ea2ecdd543-dmarc-request@list-nysac.us.
Learn why this is important
Good afternoon all -
I am looking for advice on titles in my office.  I have looked at the title on the Directors site.
First, my Deputy Director is retiring in April after 14 years in the position.  They do everything tax and V4 related.  I really would like them to pass their knowledge on before they leave.  The position is a grade 18 and after 14 years
pays about 79,000/year.   And the issues are that -
Personnel want to change the job specifications.  We hoped to begin to train a person in the office that qualifies as the job specs are now, but Personnel has said he would not be
eligible. Personnel want the change the position to non-competitive, which they are saying can take months.  I told them that many counties don't have a Deputy Director position and perhaps
we could change ours.
What similar title(s) do you have in your offices?
Next, I have a person in the office that does our 911 Addressing and maintains our 911 database.  He also reviews deeds, does some file maintenance in V4 and focuses on our counter and phones.  Doing 911 work is not in his job description,
and it used to be a full-time position of its own.
Is there a job title you might recommend for that position?
I have my work cut out for me to mend my office's relationship with Personnel.  We are meeting tomorrow and I hope to get off to a good start
😊
Thank you so much!
Tiffany
Tiffany LeRoy, Director
Schoharie County Real Property Tax Services

Schoharie, NY 12157

subject: Re: Deciphering the attached DD214 for a Veterans Exemption
body:
Looks like she only
did active duty for training.
Members
of reserves
A member of the reserve
component of the Armed Forces who was discharged or released from
active duty (beyond active duty for training), but is still a member of
the reserves, is considered a veteran for purposes of this exemption, and
is thus eligible to receive the exemption, provided that such active duty
was significant
and full-time
(see 8
Op. Counsel SBEA No. 37)
and that the veteran meets all other statutory requirements. Otherwise,
reservists are not eligible for an alternative veterans exemption.
Volume
8 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 37
Opinions
of Counsel index
Alternative veterans
exemption (member of exempt class) (reservist) - Real Property Tax Law,
§ 458-a; 38 U.S.C. § 101:
As
a general rule, reservists who engaged in active duty for training or who
were activated for short periods of time are not eligible for the alternative
veterans exemption. However, reservists who were activated during a time
of war and who performed significant, full time active duty, may qualify
for the exemption.
We have been asked
whether reservists who served on six months active duty or who were activated
for short periods of time (e.g., during a mail strike) during time
of war are eligible for the alternative veterans exemption (Real Property
Tax Law, § 458-a).
The alternative veterans
exemption may be granted to "qualifying residential real property" which
is "property owned by a qualified owner which is used exclusively for
residential purposes" (§ 458-a(1)(d)). A "qualified owner" is defined
as including a "veteran" (§ 458-a(1)(c)), that is, "a person who
served in the active military, naval, or air service during a period of
war and who was discharged or released therefrom under honorable conditions"
(§ 458-a(1)(e)).
The term "active military,
naval, or air service" is not defined in the Real Property Tax Law, but
is defined in section 101(24) of Title 38 of the United States Code (entitled
Veterans' Benefits) as including "active duty, any period of active duty
for training during which the individual concerned was disabled or died
from an injury incurred or aggravated in line of duty." The term "active
duty" is defined in section 101(21), in part, as "full time duty in the
Armed Forces, other than active duty for training." The term "active
duty for training" is defined in subdivision 22 of that section of the
U.S. Code as including "full time duty in the Armed Forces performed by
Reserves for training purposes."
From a comparison of
the definitions in new section 458-a of the RPTL and those in section 101
of Title 38 of the U.S. Code, it appears that the definitions in State
law are based upon the definitions in the Federal statute (e.g.,
compare the definition of "veteran" in RPTL, § 458-a(1)(e) and 38
U.S.C. § 101(2); see also, RPTL, § 458-a(1)(b) and 38 U.S.C.
§ 101(16) in regard to the meaning of "service connected"). Since,
as discussed above, "active military, naval, or air service" generally
excludes "active duty for training," such as full-time duty performed
by reserves for training purposes, the Federal definitions provide some
support for the conclusion that reservists who engaged in active duty for
training or who were activated for short periods of time were not intended
to be entitled to the alternative veterans exemption.
Our conclusion is further
enhanced by case law construing section 85 of New York State's Civil Service
Law which provides veterans with both additional credits on competitive
civil service exams and preference in retention upon abolition of positions.
In paragraph (a) of subdivision one of section 85, the term "veteran"
is defined as "a member of the armed forces of the United States who served
therein in time of war, [and] who was honorably discharged or released
under honorable circumstances from such service . . .". The term "armed
forces of the United States" is, in turn, defined in section 13-a of the
General Construction Law which, in part, provides that "no person shall
be considered a member or veteran of the armed forces of the United States
unless his or her service therein is or was on a full-time active duty
basis, other than active duty for training."
The courts of New York
have had occasion to construe section 85 of the Civil Service Law. In Rahill
v. Bronstein, 32 N.Y.2d 417, 298 N.E.2d 674, 345 N.Y.S.2d 534 (1973),
the Court of Appeals considered the civil service claim of several honorably
discharged members of reserve components of various branches of the armed
forces who served in those reserves during time of war. The Court held
that the scope of the civil service preference should be "limited to those
whose wartime service was 'full-time active duty'" (32 N.Y.2d at 421,
345 N.Y.S.2d at 537). While the Court noted that Article V, section 6 of
the State Constitution authorizes a preference for veterans within the
Civil Service system, it stated, "As an exception to a constitutional
mandate [in favor of civil service appointments made pursuant to merit
and fitness], the term 'member of the armed forces' should be given the
narrowest interpretation consistent with the intent of the framers" (32
N.Y.2d at 425, 345 N.Y.S.2d at 540).
Subsequently, in LaRocca
v. Bronstein, 44 A.D.2d 668, 354 N.Y.S.2d 437 (1st Dept., 1974), the
Appellate Division reversed a lower court ruling and held that the petitioner,
a member of the United States Naval Reserve in a time of war, who had served
a six month tour of active duty for training, was ineligible for a veterans
credit.
More recently, the
Court of Appeals again considered the issue in City of New York
v. City Civil Service Commission, 60 N.Y.2d 436, 458 N.E.2d 354, 470
N.Y.S.2d 113 (1983). There, the Court denied Civil Service veterans' credit
to reservists who were summoned to active duty to help maintain mail service
during a strike by postal workers in 1970. The Court held:
[U]nder
section 6 of Article V of the Constitution, and section 85 of the Civil
Service Law, veterans' credits should be awarded for civil service appointments
and promotions only where the applicant's service as a "member of the
armed forces" during a "time of war" was on a full-time basis evidencing
a sacrifice in the form of disruption of civilian life and divorce from
civilian occupation. It is not enough that an applicant's service fall
within the literal definitions of "member of armed forces" and "time
of war" if that service did not significantly interfere with the applicant's
normal employment and way of life (60 N.Y.2d at 448, 470 N.Y.S.2d at 120).
Thus, it appears that
the courts are applying a strict construction standard to the civil service
preference similar to that they apply tax exemption statutes generally
(e.g., Herkimer County v. Village of Herkimer, 251 App.Div.
126, 295 N.Y.S. 629 (4th Dept., 1937), aff'd 279 N.Y.
560, 18 N.E.2d 854 (1939)). Accordingly, based on the foregoing, it is
our opinion that reservists who engaged in active duty for training or
who were activated for short periods of time (e.g., mail strike
service) are not eligible for the alternative veterans exemption pursuant
to section 458-a of the RPTL. Reservists, however, who were activated during
a time of war and who performed significant, full-time active duty, may
qualify for the exemption.
April 18, 1985
NOTE:  In
2016, a new subdivision 10 was added to RPTL, § 458-a giving local governments
the option of granting alternative veterans exemptions to members of the
United States Armed Forces Reserves who were called to active duty to assist
the Postmaster General in restoring and maintaining postal service during
the 1970 postal strike (see L.2016, c. 476; see also L.2017,
c.141).  That activation was later designated "Operation Graphic
