Looks like she only did active duty for training.
Members of reserves
A member of the reserve component of the Armed Forces who was discharged or released from active duty (beyond active duty for training), but is still a member of the reserves, is considered a veteran
for purposes of this exemption, and is thus eligible to receive the exemption, provided that such active duty was
significant and full-time (see 8 Op. Counsel SBEA No. 37)
and that the veteran meets all other statutory requirements. Otherwise, reservists are not eligible for an alternative veterans exemption.
Volume 8 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 37
Opinions of Counsel index
Alternative veterans exemption (member of exempt class) (reservist) - Real Property Tax Law, § 458-a; 38 U.S.C. § 101:
As a general rule, reservists who engaged in active duty for training or who were activated for short periods of time are not eligible for the alternative veterans exemption. However, reservists
who were activated during a time of war and who performed significant, full time active duty, may qualify for the exemption.
We have been asked whether reservists who served on six months active duty or who were activated for short periods of time (e.g., during a mail strike) during time of war are eligible for
the alternative veterans exemption (Real Property Tax Law, § 458-a).
The alternative veterans exemption may be granted to "qualifying residential real property" which is "property owned by a qualified owner which is used exclusively for residential purposes" (§ 458-a(1)(d)).
A "qualified owner" is defined as including a "veteran" (§ 458-a(1)(c)), that is, "a person who served in the active military, naval, or air service during a period of war and who was discharged or released therefrom under honorable conditions" (§ 458-a(1)(e)).
The term "active military, naval, or air service" is not defined in the Real Property Tax Law, but is defined in section 101(24) of Title 38 of the United States Code (entitled Veterans' Benefits)
as including "active duty, any period of active duty for training during which the individual concerned was disabled or died from an injury incurred or aggravated in line of duty." The term "active duty" is defined in section 101(21), in part, as "full time
duty in the Armed Forces, other than active duty for training." The term "active duty for training" is defined in subdivision 22 of that section of the U.S. Code as including "full time duty in the Armed Forces performed by Reserves for training purposes."
From a comparison of the definitions in new section 458-a of the RPTL and those in section 101 of Title 38 of the U.S. Code, it appears that the definitions in State law are based upon the definitions
in the Federal statute (e.g., compare the definition of "veteran" in RPTL, § 458-a(1)(e) and 38 U.S.C. § 101(2); see also, RPTL, § 458-a(1)(b) and 38 U.S.C. § 101(16) in regard to the meaning of "service connected"). Since, as discussed above, "active
military, naval, or air service" generally excludes "active duty for training," such as full-time duty performed by reserves for training purposes, the Federal definitions provide some support for the conclusion that reservists who engaged in active duty for
training or who were activated for short periods of time were not intended to be entitled to the alternative veterans exemption.
Our conclusion is further enhanced by case law construing section 85 of New York State's Civil Service Law which provides veterans with both additional credits on competitive civil service exams
and preference in retention upon abolition of positions. In paragraph (a) of subdivision one of section 85, the term "veteran" is defined as "a member of the armed forces of the United States who served therein in time of war, [and] who was honorably discharged
or released under honorable circumstances from such service . . .". The term "armed forces of the United States" is, in turn, defined in section 13-a of the General Construction Law which, in part, provides that "no person shall be considered a member or veteran
of the armed forces of the United States unless his or her service therein is or was on a full-time active duty basis, other than active duty for training."
The courts of New York have had occasion to construe section 85 of the Civil Service Law. In Rahill v. Bronstein, 32 N.Y.2d 417, 298 N.E.2d 674, 345 N.Y.S.2d 534 (1973), the Court of Appeals
considered the civil service claim of several honorably discharged members of reserve components of various branches of the armed forces who served in those reserves during time of war. The Court held that the scope of the civil service preference should be
"limited to those whose wartime service was 'full-time active duty'" (32 N.Y.2d at 421, 345 N.Y.S.2d at 537). While the Court noted that Article V, section 6 of the State Constitution authorizes a preference for veterans within the Civil Service system, it
stated, "As an exception to a constitutional mandate [in favor of civil service appointments made pursuant to merit and fitness], the term 'member of the armed forces' should be given the narrowest interpretation consistent with the intent of the framers"
(32 N.Y.2d at 425, 345 N.Y.S.2d at 540).
Subsequently, in LaRocca v. Bronstein, 44 A.D.2d 668, 354 N.Y.S.2d 437 (1st Dept., 1974), the Appellate Division reversed a lower court ruling and held that the petitioner, a member of the
United States Naval Reserve in a time of war, who had served a six month tour of active duty for training, was ineligible for a veterans credit.
More recently, the Court of Appeals again considered the issue in City of New York v. City Civil Service Commission, 60 N.Y.2d 436, 458 N.E.2d 354, 470 N.Y.S.2d 113 (1983). There, the Court
denied Civil Service veterans' credit to reservists who were summoned to active duty to help maintain mail service during a strike by postal workers in 1970. The Court held:
[U]nder section 6 of Article V of the Constitution, and section 85 of the Civil Service Law, veterans' credits should be awarded for civil service appointments and promotions only where the applicant's
service as a "member of the armed forces" during a "time of war" was on a full-time basis evidencing a sacrifice in the form of disruption of civilian life and divorce from civilian occupation. It is not enough that an applicant's service fall within the literal
definitions of "member of armed forces" and "time of war" if that service did not significantly interfere with the applicant's normal employment and way of life (60 N.Y.2d at 448, 470 N.Y.S.2d at 120).
Thus, it appears that the courts are applying a strict construction standard to the civil service preference similar to that they apply tax exemption statutes generally (e.g., Herkimer
County v. Village of Herkimer, 251 App.Div. 126, 295 N.Y.S. 629 (4th Dept., 1937), aff'd 279 N.Y. 560, 18 N.E.2d 854 (1939)). Accordingly, based on the foregoing, it is our opinion that reservists who engaged in active duty for training or who were
activated for short periods of time (e.g., mail strike service) are not eligible for the alternative veterans exemption pursuant to section 458-a of the RPTL. Reservists, however, who were activated during a time of war and who performed significant,
full-time active duty, may qualify for the exemption.
April 18, 1985
NOTE:  In 2016, a new subdivision 10 was added to RPTL, § 458-a giving local governments the option of granting alternative
veterans exemptions to members of the United States Armed Forces Reserves who were called to active duty to assist the Postmaster General in restoring and maintaining postal service during the 1970 postal strike (see L.2016, c. 476; see also L.2017,
c.141).  That activation was later designated "Operation Graphic Hand."  In effect, RPTL, § 458-a(10) overrides this opinion as to reservists who served in Operation Graphic Hand, as long as their property is located in a jurisdiction that has exercised this
option and they satisfy the eligibility requirements in all other respects.  Otherwise, this opinion remains in effect.

Subject: RE: Cemetery
Kind of only 1 opinion on this:  Volume 1 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 24 but I think the "test" for exempt status is whether internments are expected within a reasonable period of time:
the cases which exempted portions of unused cemetery land indicate that the courts were satisfied that although no interments have as yet been made, the unused cemetery land would actually be used for interments within a reasonable time (People ex rel. Buffalo Burial Park Assoc. v. Stilwell, supra; St. Stanislaus Church Soc. v. Erie Co., supra).
Both court cases referenced in that opinion are by cemetery associations and I think that's pretty much the norm. The application (Form RP-446:9/08:Application for Real Property Tax Exemption for Unimproved Cemetery Land:rp446) even lists "name of organization" first so it seems clear the intention is for associations to be the owner and not just some rando.
All that being said - I would deny that COE because they would have had to file the above form with the assessor and sounds like they didn't do that and thought the deed makes a difference (which it could have...had they timely filed exempt paperwork).

Subject: Cemetery
Hey all - RPPL 450 (not RPTL) governs taxation on cemeteries. There are also opinions out there that say no one has to be even buried in them, yet, to be exempt. My question is what about ownership? Can John Smith break off 20 acres of his land and say there will be a cemetery there?
I have an association (not a cemetery one) that claims they are a 501(c)(3). They own hundreds of acres and broke off 14 for a supposed cemetery. They wrote in their deed that it was for that. This was last year so now they are asking for a COE because it was never made exempt. For a little background, this was supposed to be a commune of sorts back in the 60's. Today is just trash buildings, tires everywhere, and vacant land. Maybe 20 people living on 800 acres.
Thoughts?

CAUTION:
Kind of only 1 opinion on this:  Volume 1 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 24 but I think the "test" for exempt status is whether internments are expected within a reasonable period of time:
the cases which exempted portions of unused cemetery land indicate that the courts were satisfied that although no interments have as yet been made, the unused cemetery land would actually be used for interments within a reasonable time (People ex rel. Buffalo Burial Park Assoc. v. Stilwell, supra; St. Stanislaus Church Soc. v. Erie Co., supra).
Both court cases referenced in that opinion are by cemetery associations and I think that's pretty much the norm. The application (Form RP-446:9/08:Application for Real Property Tax Exemption for Unimproved Cemetery Land:rp446) even lists "name of organization" first so it seems clear the intention is for associations to be the owner and not just some rando.
All that being said - I would deny that COE because they would have had to file the above form with the assessor and sounds like they didn't do that and thought the deed makes a difference (which it could have...had they timely filed exempt paperwork).

Hey all - RPPL 450 (not RPTL) governs taxation on cemeteries. There are also opinions out there that say no one has to be even buried in them, yet, to be exempt. My question is what about ownership? Can John Smith break off 20 acres of his land and say there will be a cemetery there?
I have an association (not a cemetery one) that claims they are a 501(c)(3). They own hundreds of acres and broke off 14 for a supposed cemetery. They wrote in their deed that it was for that. This was last year so now they are asking for a COE because it was never made exempt. For a little background, this was supposed to be a commune of sorts back in the 60's. Today is just trash buildings, tires everywhere, and vacant land. Maybe 20 people living on 800 acres.
Thoughts?

subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] Re: [ EXTERNAL ]  Re: Courtesy split/subdivision?
body:
I've heard some issues with suffixed (leased land) parcels going to foreclosure/tax sale, but they can be situation-specific. Like we have privately owned suffixed parcels on NYS land--the drama that ensues when the home/camp owners don't pay their taxes and
we try to put them onto the auction eligible list is impressive. This fall we had to start the process of negotiating an agreement with NYS for those situations, because they're privately owned, but also kinda not, because their "ownership" is based on an
agreement with NYS, so if NYS doesn't re-agree with a new owner, then the sale fizzles. Also mobile homes in a park--can't foreclose on a single wide trailer if someone can just move it out of the town, and those parcels don't include the land, so there's no
recourse.
That said...those types of parcels would be difficult to sell anyway, if they went to auction, and we don't have a lot of them (proportionally) here, so we don't worry about the suffixed/non-suffixed issue too much.

This is exactly why I discourage suffixed parcels. We have had a few scenarios where our treasurer cannot foreclose on suffixed parcels as legally, they do not exist. Our solar is put on the parent parcel and it is all on one tax bill unless the legal subdivision
process has been done. If the land owner has done their own due diligence then they will be protected in their lease with the solar company for how the taxes will be broken down. It sounds harsh but it protects the municipalities, county, and schools from
having issues with tax collection if it comes down to that.

Hi Trish,
All of my cell towers are not separated, but inclusive within the parcel. The parcel is billed in full. Our office provides an annual assessment apportionment
letter to the property owner. They in turn, use the assessment apportionment for reimbursement from the companies. We are responsible for the apportionment of the assessments, but not producing a tax bill.  The owner's addresses the tax calculation with the
companies; we do not provide a tax bill.  Property owners and companies use the rates on the tax bill against the assessment apportionment to determine the companies tax liability reimbursement. There has never been an issue with the procedure.
I believe it was designed that way, because if a tax foreclosure took place, the entire property would be encumbered, not just a fraction of it.

However, my solar farm is leasing 5 acres of the Town's tax exempt capped land fill which solar farm is under a PILOT with a fixed annual payment so I will also be doing
an artificial split for the solar farm on the 5 acres separate and apart from the remaining tax exempt Town owned capped land fill,

subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] Re: S.1183 Veterans Exemption Updated
body:
I haven't seen anything saying "definitely don't do it for 2026 roll," and I know
of places that are still considering it, if they can get it in place before 3/1, to give their disabled veterans a chance at the exemption for an extra year (I guess if they file some sort of proof/application prior to 3/1, even if we don't have an official
application for this version specifically, or additional guidance from ORPTS, they'd have met the application requirements and the assessor has until roll time to get more info).
In terms of RPS, if we don't get an update before tentative roll, I think a workaround would just be adding a new (temporary) exemption code--I'd probably make it a 5xxxx_ code, so it will show up in reports as a "system code" and not get lost, but you can label
it with the RPTL reference and change it on the parcels once RPS is updated. That said, I'm sure we'll get something before tentative roll. They didn't give dates in the RPS Governance meeting when we asked, so it may be cutting it close, lol, but I'd guess
an April update with that and the senior exempt percent updates.

made, the unused cemetery land would actually be used for interments within a reasonable time (People ex rel. Buffalo Burial Park Assoc. v. Stilwell, supra; St. Stanislaus Church Soc. v. Erie Co., supra).
Both court cases referenced in that opinion are by cemetery associations and I think that's pretty much the norm. The application (Form
RP-446:9/08:Application for Real Property Tax Exemption for Unimproved Cemetery Land:rp446) even lists "name of organization" first so it seems clear the intention is for associations to be the owner and not just some rando.
All that being said - I would deny that COE because they would have had to file the above form with the assessor and sounds like they didn't do that and thought the deed makes a difference (which it could
have...had they timely filed exempt paperwork).

Hey all - RPPL 450 (not RPTL) governs taxation on cemeteries. There are also opinions out there that say no one has to be even buried in them, yet, to be exempt. My question is what about ownership? Can John Smith break off 20 acres of
his land and say there will be a cemetery there?
I have an association (not a cemetery one) that claims they are a 501(c)(3). They own hundreds of acres and broke off 14 for a supposed cemetery. They wrote in their deed that it was for that. This was last year so now they are asking for
a COE because it was never made exempt. For a little background, this was supposed to be a commune of sorts back in the 60's. Today is just trash buildings, tires everywhere, and vacant land. Maybe 20 people living on 800 acres.

I'm reading the table for the Senior exemption amendment (see below) and find it confusing. It appears that there are "holes/gaps"

subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] Re: S.1183 Veterans Exemption Updated
body:
I don't think it's a duplicate, I think it's an "extension" of the existing law. Or at least that's how I explained it to my CFO and County Exec (and the lawyer didn't disagree, so I don't think I steered them wrong). Our existing disabled vets is capped at
50%, this is 100%, just with stricter rules. And I would have to look at it again, but I think there's no value cap associated. So, currently if a vet has a 100% disability rating and a house worth $300k, they will get our county's maximum of $120k for the
disabled, then whatever max for the wartime/combatzone exemption, but still have to pay on $150k or so. If they qualified for this new one, then that cap is gone.
I know plenty of folks will ALSO have other exemptions like low income disabled or senior, but if we're talking about a disabled vet whose spouse or sibling owns the house with them and is bringing in $75k a year, they wouldn't
get those.
I think it would make more sense if it had been advertised/worded differently. Not as a new thing, but as an increase to benefits for only those with the highest of accommodation needs. "If you have a 100% disability rating, AND are considered permanently and
totally disabled, AND qualify for or receive VA benefits, you are eligible for the "disabled vet 2.0" edition of the exemption, where it's 100% off and there's no value cap.
I have no idea if we have anyone who would qualify, tbh. Definitely fewer than people seem to believe (I've already had one person get cranky at me because I told him in casual conversation in the office that he wouldn't qualify, with his 80% disability rating
and having a full time job--we've gotten several calls about it too, where the callers seem to think "I'm disabled and I'm a veteran, I want free taxes" is the only eligibility criteria).

subject: Re: Cemetery
body:
Some people who received this message don't often get email from corey.metz@oswegocountyny.gov.
Learn why this is important
Kind of only 1 opinion on this:
Volume 1 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 24 but I think the "test" for exempt status is whether internments are expected within a reasonable period of time:
the cases which exempted portions of unused cemetery land indicate that the courts were satisfied that although no interments have as yet been
made, the unused cemetery land would actually be used for interments within a reasonable time (People ex rel. Buffalo Burial Park Assoc. v. Stilwell, supra; St. Stanislaus Church Soc. v. Erie Co., supra).
Both court cases referenced in that opinion are by cemetery associations and I think that's pretty much the norm. The application (Form
RP-446:9/08:Application for Real Property Tax Exemption for Unimproved Cemetery Land:rp446) even lists "name of organization" first so it seems clear the intention is for associations to be the owner and not just some rando.
All that being said - I would deny that COE because they would have had to file the above form with the assessor and sounds like they didn't do that and thought the deed makes a difference (which
it could have...had they timely filed exempt paperwork).
Corey Metz
(She/her/hers)
Director | REAL
PROPERTY TAX SERVICES
46 East Bridge Street Oswego NY 13126
Website: oswegocounty.com/rpts
Office: (315) 349-8315 | Direct: 8280

On Behalf Of Daniel T. Martonis
Sent: Wednesday, November 5, 2025 12:42 PM
To: RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US
Subject: Cemetery
Hey all - RPPL 450 (not RPTL) governs taxation on cemeteries. There are also opinions out there that say no one has to be even buried in them, yet, to be exempt. My question is what about ownership? Can John Smith break off 20 acres of
his land and say there will be a cemetery there?
I have an association (not a cemetery one) that claims they are a 501(c)(3). They own hundreds of acres and broke off 14 for a supposed cemetery. They wrote in their deed that it was for that. This was last year so now they are asking for
a COE because it was never made exempt. For a little background, this was supposed to be a commune of sorts back in the 60's. Today is just trash buildings, tires everywhere, and vacant land. Maybe 20 people living on 800 acres.
Thoughts?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Daniel T. Martonis
Director of Real Property Tax Services
Chairman, Cattaraugus County Land Bank
Cattaraugus County

Little Valley, NY 14755

subject: Advice Needed
body:
I have an RP 554 that has been submitted to my office wherein the owner of the property is alleging that the Assessor should have used a different methodology to calculate the assessed value of that property. The property in question meets
the requirements of RPTL 581A and the property owner is alleging that a Clerical Error occurred as per RPTL 550 2j.
I believe that the property owner has a valid case that the property should have an assessment calculated via the methodology in 581A. However, the applicant never submitted the paperwork to the Assessor for her to make such a determination
before taxable status date.
Is there a statute that I can point to that says that the property owner must provide paperwork to the Assessor in order to qualify for this new assessment calculation methodology?
Vic
Victor L. Mallison
Executive Director
Westchester County Tax Commission
110 MLK Blvd, Room 346
White Plains, NY 10601
(914) 995-4325

subject: Re: Advice Needed
body:
Hey Vic,
There was a court case in Tioga County about this a few years ago and the gist was that the assessor is supposed to know about this and that the PO has no responsibility to provide something
to the assessor.  I think it was a conversion project of a prior school building.  This is why it was done under the COE process as opposed to having to go to the BAR.
Maybe Steve remembers the name of it.  But checking the law book, the notes indicate the 3rd Dept base about the Warrensburg Commons LPT vs Town of Warrensburg assessor might also
be good to look at.

subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] Re: Advice Needed
body:
Some people who received this message don't often get email from 00000106db98a9de-dmarc-request@list-nysac.us.
Learn why this is important
The case is here:
Matter of Warrensburg Commons LPT v Town Assessor of Town of Warrensburg :: 2010 :: New York Appellate Division, Third Department Decisions :: New York Case Law :: New York Law :: U.S. Law :: Justia
Reads to me that the Court wasn't willing to infer a forfeiture of the 581-a valuation method if income statements aren't submitted annually because the law didn't clearly define what to do in that scenario, so they sided with the Petitioner:
"The Legislature has provided provisions in other parts of the RPTL whereby a property owner forfeits or does not obtain a right because of failure to act within a certain
time frame (see e.g. RPTL 425, 525 [2] [a]; 718 [2] [d]). In the absence of such a provision in this statute, we decline to create one by inference."
I have a similar situation in City of Fulton right now where an attorney is harassing the assessor to correct the past 3 rolls because their client has a building subject to 581-a, but the owners
stipulated with the Assessor each year. I'm waiting for the inevitable RP-556 to wind up on my desk...

Caution: This is an external email. Please take care when clicking links or opening attachments. When in doubt, contact the Help Desk.
The case is here:
Matter of Warrensburg Commons LPT v Town Assessor of Town of Warrensburg :: 2010 :: New York Appellate Division, Third Department Decisions :: New York Case Law :: New York Law :: U.S. Law :: Justia
Reads to me that the Court wasn't willing to infer a forfeiture of the 581-a valuation method if income statements aren't submitted annually because the law didn't clearly define what to do in that scenario, so they sided with the Petitioner:
"The Legislature has provided provisions in other parts of the RPTL whereby a property owner forfeits or does not obtain a right because of failure to act within a certain time frame
(see e.g. RPTL 425, 525 [2] [a]; 718 [2] [d]). In the absence of such a provision in this statute, we decline to create one by inference."
I have a similar situation in City of Fulton right now where an attorney is harassing the assessor to correct the past 3 rolls because their client has a building subject to 581-a, but the owners stipulated
with the Assessor each year. I'm waiting for the inevitable RP-556 to wind up on my desk...

subject: PILOT Agreement on Solar Projects
body:
Some people who received this message don't often get email from 00000114281fcc00-dmarc-request@list-nysac.us.
Learn why this is important
Good morning,
Does anyone have PILOT Agreements on Solar Projects in your area?  These would not be under the traditional 487 PILOT, which is between the taxing entity and the developer, but the IDA PILOT which is between the IDA and the developer.
If you have an IDA PILOT in your region, do you count the land underneath as exempt along with the improvements if the agreement specifies to do so?  And how do you assess the land underneath the solar project improvement?  Have you included
the land and improvements under a new tax map number?  Does it normally stay with the parent parcel or does it go with the improvements?  Trying to verify that we are accurately mapping and assessing these IDA PILOT Agreement solar projects correctly.
Thank you!
Emily Wilson
Director of Real Property
St. Lawrence County
Real Property
48 Court Street
Canton, N.Y.  13617
Phone: 315-229-3226

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) PILOT Agreement on Solar Projects
body:
Here, land never goes with any of our IDA PILOTs. That includes those for solar (all our solar are IDA PILOTs). We suffix out the solar equipment onto its own exempt parcel. We then value the land based on
the income approach using the lease as the basis. The land ends up being around 20k/acre.
If the IDA writes in that the land is included, then I would have a word with that IDA. It shouldn't be, but I don't know all their laws.
We have used solar workshops and our Ag & Farmland board to get the word out to farmers about the increase in value. All of their leases have clauses written in to pay any increase in tax due to increase in
land value. Make sure yours knows to do this as well.
Daniel T. Martonis

subject: Re: PILOT Agreement on Solar Projects
body:
Emily,
Attached is a copy of a recent IDA PILOT for a solar farm in Lewis County, it does not include the land under it.  Unless the developer owns the land, I don't know how that could be included in the PILOT.
Like Dan in Cattaraugus, we suffix the parcel to include the improvements, including the fencing around the array.  The land value is increased on the parent parcel and classed as commercial land as it becomes
income producing.  Some leases between the landowner and the developer have a clause that the developer will pay any increases in taxes due to the increase in land value but that is separate from the PILOT agreement and the bill still goes to the landowner
for the land.  How they arrange payment from the developer is between them.
I've seen where some counties depict the leased area on the tax maps as a shaded area or thatched lines.  We have not incorporated that into our maps yet, but I do like the idea of being able to identify the
area on the map.  We do have one property owner that split the leased area from his farm parcel, but he still gets the tax bill for the leased land and it is in his name.
Candy Akin, CCD
Real Property Tax Director
2025-2026 President, NYSACDRPTS
O: 315-376-5336
M: 315-907-2032
candyakin@lewiscounty.ny.gov

Subject: PILOT Agreement on Solar Projects
Good morning,
Does anyone have PILOT Agreements on Solar Projects in your area?  These would not be under the traditional 487 PILOT, which is between the taxing entity and the developer, but the IDA PILOT which is between the IDA and the developer.
If you have an IDA PILOT in your region, do you count the land underneath as exempt along with the improvements if the agreement specifies to do so?  And how do you assess the land underneath the solar project improvement?  Have you included
the land and improvements under a new tax map number?  Does it normally stay with the parent parcel or does it go with the improvements?  Trying to verify that we are accurately mapping and assessing these IDA PILOT Agreement solar projects correctly.
Thank you!

subject: FW: Deed question?
body:
I am being asked by one of the Assessors in my County if it is ok to move the Greivance Day from the Third Tuesday in June in one of his Towns. This Assessor represents two Towns and cannot be in more than one place at a time. The only thing I could find in the County Law was the following.
Sec. 283.121. - Completion and verification of assessment roll; notice of hearing to review assessments.
1. The assessor or the assessors, as herein provided, shall complete and verify the assessment roll on the first day of June
of each year, make out a copy thereof to be left in the office of the town clerk and forthwith cause a notice to be conspicuously posted in three or more public places in the tax district and cause to be published a similar notice in at least one newspaper
either published in such town or having a general circulation therein, stating that he or they have completed the assessment roll and that a copy thereof has been left at the office of the town clerk where it may be seen
and examined by any person until the third Tuesday of June in each year, and that on that day the assessors or board of review, as the case may be,
will meet at a time and place specified in such notice for the purpose of reviewing any such assessment at the instance of any interested party. A board of review shall meet on the third Tuesday of June in each year and
thereafter continue to meet at such time or times as may be necessary and appropriate to consider and determine the objections or grievances filed against the assessments, and in such town the notice of hearing shall
so state.
State Law only seems to say, "On the date required by law, the  board  of  assessment  review  shall  meet  to  hear  complaints  in  relation  to assessments."
Could they set a local law in their Town to change the date?
Victor L. Mallison
Executive Director
Westchester County Tax Commission
110 MLK Blvd, Room 346
White Plains, NY 10601

"1-a. The governing body of an assessing unit which employs an assessor

I am being asked by one of the Assessors in my County if it is ok to move the Greivance Day from the Third Tuesday in June in one of his Towns. This Assessor represents two Towns and cannot be in more than one place at a time. The only thing I could find in the County Law was the following.
Sec. 283.121. - Completion and verification of assessment roll; notice of hearing to review assessments.
1. The assessor or the assessors, as herein provided, shall complete and verify the assessment roll
on the first day of June of each year, make out a copy thereof to be left in the office of the town clerk and forthwith cause a notice to be conspicuously posted in three or more public places in the tax district and cause to be published a similar notice
in at least one newspaper either published in such town or having a general circulation therein, stating that he or they have completed the assessment roll and that a copy thereof has been left at the office of the town
clerk where it may be seen and examined by any person until the third Tuesday of June in each year, and that on that day the assessors or board of
review, as the case may be, will meet at a time and place specified in such notice for the purpose of reviewing any such assessment at the instance of any interested party. A board of review shall meet on the third Tuesday
of June in each year and thereafter continue to meet at such time or times as may be necessary and appropriate to consider and determine the objections or grievances filed against the assessments, and in such town the
notice of hearing shall so state.
State Law only seems to say, "On the date required by law, the  board  of  assessment  review  shall  meet  to  hear  complaints  in  relation  to assessments."
Could they set a local law in their Town to change the date?

subject: Re: PILOT Agreement on Solar Projects
body:
Hi Emily,
All of our PILOT agreements for solar projects through our IDA have had leaseback agreements.  We do a split for the land with the solar project, ownership of the parcel is not changed, but split allows exemption
to be applied to land and improvement.  PILOT agreements includes a base valuation payment, but at assessed value of the land prior to completion of the project.
☹
I had assumed this was standard and never questioned.  Although, the alternative is to create a suffix for the solar improvement, which we only create suffix parcels if absolutely necessary.

land owner asking to remove the acreage from his tax bill due to the agreement between the IDA and the developer stating that the
"Equipment and, together with the Land and Improvements are classified as the Facility" and the agreement later states that the Facility shall be exempt from Real Estate Taxes.
At the moment, almost all of our IDA PILOTs for solar projects are mapped and classified the way the responses I have received are and the land below is valued as leased land and kept with the property owner as it is still in their name.
We only one or two that we have split with the land underneath was when the actual property owners sold the land to the developer.

RE: Candy's last point about depicting it on the tax map, that's how we've been doing it here for a few years. This is what it looks like:
https://arcg.is/0GGGyK1
(you can swap to the tax map by clicking the square in the bottom left of the map area)
Our mapper set it up by simply adding in a boolean field to the GIS files called 'fee' where 0 means it's not a fee parcel (i.e. leased land) and 1 is the default (parcel is fee). Then it's just a matter of symbolizing the parcels differently based on whether
or not they're fee.

Emily,
Attached is a copy of a recent IDA PILOT for a solar farm in Lewis County, it does not include the land under it.  Unless the developer owns the land, I don't know how that could be included in the PILOT.
Like Dan in Cattaraugus, we suffix the parcel to include the improvements, including the fencing around the array.  The land value is increased on the parent parcel and classed as commercial land as it becomes
income producing.  Some leases between the landowner and the developer have a clause that the developer will pay any increases in taxes due to the increase in land value but that is separate from the PILOT agreement and the bill still goes to the landowner
for the land.  How they arrange payment from the developer is between them.
I've seen where some counties depict the leased area on the tax maps as a shaded area or thatched lines.  We have not incorporated that into our maps yet, but I do like the idea of being able to identify the
area on the map.  We do have one property owner that split the leased area from his farm parcel, but he still gets the tax bill for the leased land and it is in his name.

Subject: Returned check - Account Closed
Good morning~
We have encountered another instance where a check was processed incorrectly, resulting in the customer's check
being returned with the notation "Account Closed." Upon review, the account number on the check does not match the account number that was submitted. Although the check is stamped "Account Closed," this payment needs to be resubmitted correctly without imposing
any additional fees on the customer or the County.
This collection period has seen a significant number of errors related to incorrect MICR line entries, which has
caused considerable frustration among taxpayers. To prevent these issues, we recommend implementing a verification process before returning any check to Real Property to ensure that the submission was accurate.
It appears that these errors occur primarily when account information must be entered manually because the check
reader cannot read the MICR line. This step is critical to ensure the correct account number is used for payment.  We need to establish a clear checks-and-balances procedure verify account details before returning checks to the county as insufficient, regardless
of the reason.
Our office has been receiving numerous calls and complaints, which our customer service team is addressing, though
these issues are beyond our control.
Thank you for your attention to this matter. Please let me know if you need additional details or assistance in
implementing a solution.
Wendy

Issue: A church owns a house. This house is within a very heavy tourist area for skiing (Ellicottville). They have their church nearby as well, but not on the same property. The assessor has it exempt and has been lenient with them as they
figure out what they wish to do with the house. Well, we just found out that they rented it out all last year to private individuals. Now the assessor is demanding the exemption application and details of what their plan is. They are saying that they use it
for "youth groups" and "bible study." They also let the kids ski after these sessions. They say they don't use the church for these reasons because the house has a shower (ummm, okay).
I'm thinking that maybe just a portion of the house should be exempt.
There are so many court cases out there that deal with parts of this issue. That's why I'm asking you all.
Thanks in advance.
Daniel T. Martonis

sophospsmartbannerend
Hey all - RPPL 450 (not RPTL) governs taxation on cemeteries. There are also opinions out there that say no one has to be even buried in them, yet, to be exempt. My question is what about ownership? Can John Smith break off 20 acres of
his land and say there will be a cemetery there?
I have an association (not a cemetery one) that claims they are a 501(c)(3). They own hundreds of acres and broke off 14 for a supposed cemetery. They wrote in their deed that it was for that. This was last year so now they are asking for
a COE because it was never made exempt. For a little background, this was supposed to be a commune of sorts back in the 60's. Today is just trash buildings, tires everywhere, and vacant land. Maybe 20 people living on 800 acres.
Thoughts?

subject: Re: Religion and Houses
body:
Several years ago, a similar occurrence.
Woman died and gifted 2 lakefront seasonal properties to a Baptist church based in South Carolina. The church claimed they used both properties for retreats, etc. Assessor placed both properties on the roll when he discovered they were listing and hosting the
properties as STR's for $300/night and were booked for most weeks in the summer. Church challenged the assessments and the assessor/town lost. Superior Court Judge ruled, "if they say it's church purposes, it's church purposes."
Best,
Barry

Subject: Re: Religion and Houses
Several years ago, a similar occurrence.
Woman died and gifted 2 lakefront seasonal properties to a Baptist church based in South Carolina. The church claimed they used both properties for retreats, etc. Assessor
placed both properties on the roll when he discovered they were listing and hosting the properties as STR's for $300/night and were booked for most weeks in the summer. Church challenged the assessments and the assessor/town lost. Superior Court Judge ruled,
"if they say it's church purposes, it's church purposes."
Best,
Barry

Sent: Wednesday, February 18, 2026 2:44 PM

Subject: Religion and Houses
This message originated from outside of the organization.
I'm wondering if anyone has anything similar and how you're handling it...
Issue: A church owns a house. This house is within a very heavy tourist area for skiing (Ellicottville). They have their church nearby as well, but not on the same property. The assessor has it exempt and has been lenient with them as
they figure out what they wish to do with the house. Well, we just found out that they rented it out all last year to private individuals. Now the assessor is demanding the exemption application and details of what their plan is. They are saying that they
use it for "youth groups" and "bible study." They also let the kids ski after these sessions. They say they don't use the church for these reasons because the house has a shower (ummm, okay).
I'm thinking that maybe just a portion of the house should be exempt.
There are so many court cases out there that deal with parts of this issue. That's why I'm asking you all.
Thanks in advance.
Daniel T. Martonis

Hey all - RPPL 450 (not RPTL) governs taxation on cemeteries. There are also opinions out there that say no one has to be even buried in them, yet, to be exempt. My question is what about ownership? Can John Smith break off 20 acres of his land and say there will be a cemetery there?
I have an association (not a cemetery one) that claims they are a 501(c)(3). They own hundreds of acres and broke off 14 for a supposed cemetery. They wrote in their deed that it was for that. This was last year so now they are asking for a COE because it was never made exempt. For a little background, this was supposed to be a commune of sorts back in the 60's. Today is just trash buildings, tires everywhere, and vacant land. Maybe 20 people living on 800 acres.
Thoughts?

subject: 100% Vet Question
body:
I've attached the S8803 Amended bill.  In the below section that has all of the buzz, I thought that there was wording that said that the modifications had to be approved by the Veteran's Administration/US Govt?  I thought I read that somewhere.
However, seeing S8803, it does NOT specify that here.  So, the way I'm now reading this is that the discharge has to be approved by the US Govt, the disability has to be approved by the US Govt, they need to be declared fully unemployable by same, and must
have used some of their assistance money to do some handicap accessible improvements to their home (see in yellow).  It does not specify that these improvements be approved by the US Govt (like the rest of the requirements), nor does it specify as to what
level of improvements are required to receive this designation/exemption.  So, could one receive assistance money and then go and hire the least costly handyman to build a handicap accessible ramp to the front of their home and be good to go with this exemption?
....... and 5 (iv) who is eligible for pecuniary assistance from the United States government, or has received pecuniary assistance from the United States government
and has applied such assistance toward the acquisition or modification of a suitable housing unit with special features or movable facilities made necessary by the nature of the veterans' disability,
and  the necessary [law] land therefor shall be fully exempt from taxation and special district charges, assessments and special ad valorem levies, provided that such veteran meets all other requirements of this section.
Thanks, Trish

subject: Re: BAR Online training
body:
After things started getting back to normal after Covid, I continued to do my BAR training via Zoom for quite a few years. I shared the state's power point on my screen, and
I could see by the members cameras that they actually attended for the whole thing. That worked pretty well.
Last year was the first year that I went back to doing it in-person, and I am doing it that way this year. The zoom option may work best for some people.
I have occasionally had people that absolutely couldn't fit in my or any nearby trainings. I did have them watch the state's 3-hour video and sign a document confirming that
they watched it. Honestly, it would take less time out of their life to attend the training, as it seldom goes 3 hours.
Anyway, I only gave this option to members that have been on the BAR before. New members had to attend either my or another county's training.
I much prefer when they can attend a training, whether it is in-person or via Zoom because we get some good discussions going, and I can emphasis certain points.
Going to see how this year goes, and then decide whether to go back to the zoom training next year. Both have their advantages and disadvantages!
~ Meghan.

subject: Cemetery
body:
Hey all - RPPL 450 (not RPTL) governs taxation on cemeteries. There are also opinions out there that say no one has to be even buried in them, yet, to be exempt. My question is what about ownership? Can John Smith break off 20 acres of
his land and say there will be a cemetery there?
I have an association (not a cemetery one) that claims they are a 501(c)(3). They own hundreds of acres and broke off 14 for a supposed cemetery. They wrote in their deed that it was for that. This was last year so now they are asking for
a COE because it was never made exempt. For a little background, this was supposed to be a commune of sorts back in the 60's. Today is just trash buildings, tires everywhere, and vacant land. Maybe 20 people living on 800 acres.
Thoughts?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Daniel T. Martonis
Director of Real Property Tax Services
Chairman, Cattaraugus County Land Bank
Cattaraugus County
Real Property Tax Services
207 Rock City Street, Suite 101
Little Valley, NY 14755
Phone: (716) 938-2324

subject: Re: BAR Online training
body:
I did the power point on a big screen in a conference room last year and stopped for conversation, but everyone looked bored to death, even though we had a few stories, but I found that when someone went on too long, people were fidgeting, like 'come on, let's
go, we want to get out of here'. So I just feel like I won't do that again, I'd rather them just watch the video/powerpoint in their own space and time.
Get Outlook for iOS

After things started getting back to normal after Covid, I continued to do my BAR training via Zoom for quite a few years. I shared the state's power point on my screen,
and I could see by the members cameras that they actually attended for the whole thing. That worked pretty well.
Last year was the first year that I went back to doing it in-person, and I am doing it that way this year. The zoom option may work best for some people.
I have occasionally had people that absolutely couldn't fit in my or any nearby trainings. I did have them watch the state's 3-hour video and sign a document confirming
that they watched it. Honestly, it would take less time out of their life to attend the training, as it seldom goes 3 hours.
Anyway, I only gave this option to members that have been on the BAR before. New members had to attend either my or another county's training.
I much prefer when they can attend a training, whether it is in-person or via Zoom because we get some good discussions going, and I can emphasis certain points.
Going to see how this year goes, and then decide whether to go back to the zoom training next year. Both have their advantages and disadvantages!
~ Meghan.

After things started getting back to normal after Covid, I continued to do my BAR training via Zoom for quite a few years. I shared the state's power point on my screen, and
I could see by the members cameras that they actually attended for the whole thing. That worked pretty well.
Last year was the first year that I went back to doing it in-person, and I am doing it that way this year. The zoom option may work best for some people.
I have occasionally had people that absolutely couldn't fit in my or any nearby trainings. I did have them watch the state's 3-hour video and sign a document confirming that
they watched it. Honestly, it would take less time out of their life to attend the training, as it seldom goes 3 hours.
Anyway, I only gave this option to members that have been on the BAR before. New members had to attend either my or another county's training.
I much prefer when they can attend a training, whether it is in-person or via Zoom because we get some good discussions going, and I can emphasis certain points.
Going to see how this year goes, and then decide whether to go back to the zoom training next year. Both have their advantages and disadvantages!
~ Meghan.

I have occasionally had people that absolutely couldn't fit in my or any nearby trainings. I did have them watch the state's 3-hour video and sign a document confirming that
they watched it. Honestly, it would take less time out of their life to attend the training, as it seldom goes 3 hours.
Anyway, I only gave this option to members that have been on the BAR before. New members had to attend either my or another county's training.
I much prefer when they can attend a training, whether it is in-person or via Zoom because we get some good discussions going, and I can emphasis certain points.
Going to see how this year goes, and then decide whether to go back to the zoom training next year. Both have their advantages and disadvantages!

subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] RPTL 305(2)
body:
I would steer her to the ORPS site and tell her to read all of the links on the "Learn about assessments and property taxes" page:
https://www.tax.ny.gov/pit/property/propertyowners.htm
and especially all of the links on the Contest your assessment page, including the videos at the bottom:
https://www.tax.ny.gov/pit/property/contest/contestasmt.htm
And if that doesn't take the wind out of her sails and completely remove her will to live, then have her explain the assessment calendar, including the different roll dates, in a 1,000 word essay.

Hello There is a tax payer accusing the assessor of potentially breaking RPTL 305(2). The town has an eq. rate of 70. The subdivision this person lives in has been developed since the last town-wide r
sophospsmartbannerend
Hello
There is a tax payer accusing the assessor of potentially breaking RPTL 305(2).
The town has an eq. rate of 70.  The subdivision this person lives in has been developed since the last town-wide revaluation.  The property owner is stating that the assessor is breaking the law because her fair market value exceeds the actual fair market value.  This entire subdivision is potentially over valued because they are all newly built homes with next to no resales since the original  purchase.
The assessor and I have explained at length the process she needs to follow to protest her assessment.  She just doesn't want to listen and insists that the AV be reduced NOW without trying or wanting to understand this isn't possible at this time.  She thinks that if she completes the grievance form now it should be reviewed and changed now.  I have suggested an appraisal be completed and the assessor review it for a possible reduction to the 26 roll.
Who has any suggestions to better explain and help this property owner understand what she needs to do going forward?
Any suggestions are greatly appreciated.
Have a great evening
Karen Ambroz  Director
Wayne County Real Property Tax Services
16 William St
Lyons  NY  14489
Phone: 315.946.5922
Fax:
KAmbroz@waynecountyny.gov

subject: Re: EXTERNAL Senior Exemption
body:
They do not need to submit a new application.  Once adopted by local law/resolution the new income levels would go into effect.  Just note that RPS
does not currently have a patch to allow for an exemption at a percentage greater than 50%.  ORPTS is working on this currently.

subject: What constitutes "error in essential fact"?
body:
I have an assessor who has, in the past, made assessment stipulations/changes after tentative roll (and even after final roll), so when we got a correction request to lower an AV from $1,020,700 to $400,000 because "partial assessment increased as a completed
property...per photos of inside given to assessor property is not completed inside" I was cautious to allow it without double checking. This is a big reduction and will mean going to our already contentious county legislature asking them to approve a reduction
of nearly $20,000 between the school and county/town taxes (which they hadn't paid). In the grand scheme of huge budgets, spread across 3 entities, it's not a lot, but with things sometimes getting heated in the legislature, I want to be certain in what we
send to them! In your opinions, is this an error in essential fact that we just approve, since the assessor signed off on it, or is it a "they should have gone to BAR/SCAR" situation?
Thanks!

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) What constitutes "error in essential fact"?
body:
You're dealing with a couple of different timelines with this "error."
If it's after tentative but before final, then the error should go on a 552. If it's lowering an assessment, they can use a 524 as well. In either case, these have to go in front of the BAR. You have no say
in it.
If it's after final, then it's either a 553, 554, or 556 depending on the timing. You have no say in the 553, but you have to do your research for the 554 and 556. If this "error" came in on one of those,
then it's up to you to give your recommendation as to if you agree, or disagree, with it. This is the only time that you have actual power. You can ask the assessor to give you everything they can about the correction, including the photos that they mention.
You can ask to see their files at the town hall. You can also ask the owner for the information (go around a contentious assessor if you wish). In truth, the assessor shouldn't even be in the chain of a correction unless you ask them to. In real life, we know
that the person is probably going to them first.
If their response, or actions, don't satisfy you, then recommend a denial. It's ultimately up to your legislature then.
For a blanket statement, I have recommended corrections due to percent complete as of taxable status day. I have also denied them due to lack of proof.

subject: Leasehold/Possessory Interest – Certificate of Transfer
body:
Hi all,
I'm looking for some guidance on a situation involving a Town owned parcel where an individual previously held a leasehold/possessory interest. From what I can tell, the fee ownership of the parcel has always remained with the Town. The
individual held a leasehold or possessory interest, so the the parcel has been carried in RPS as a "slash account" reflecting both the municipal owner and the lessee on the assessment roll. That slash account parcel received a tax bill in the individual's
name.
Recently, the attorney sent me a  "Certificate of Transfer of Title to Leased Property and Lease Assignment and Assumption" (USPS form), and is now asking that we change the owner name on the 2026 town/county tax bill to reflect the Town.
However, nothing was ever filed with our office or the County Clerk prior to tax bill production.  I'm not sure how I would handle this or if changing the name on the tax bill is something I can even do. Has anyone else dealt with something similar to this?
Thank you,
Victoria Blancato
Director, Real Property Tax Services
Wyoming County
143 North Main Street, Warsaw, NY 14569
Phone: (585) 786-8828 | Email: vblancato@wyomingcountyny.gov
https://www.wyomingcountyny.gov/

subject: Re: Leasehold/Possessory Interest – Certificate of Transfer
body:
I would never change the owner on the tax bill - it is what it is.  If the town wanted to print a new bill with the new 'owner', they can go right ahead.  But once I print bills, I'm not reprinting
them.  And if the person doesn't have an interest in the property - what do they care that their name is on the bill?  They have no responsibility to pay it.
I would contact the town to confirm that there is no longer a leasehold interest in this parcel and if such, direct the assessor to remove the slash account.  Nothing needs to be recorded to
be legal so if it's not recorded, checking with the town is easiest way to find out if what someone is telling you is true.

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) What constitutes "error in essential fact"?
body:
Yes, the taxpayer came forward this week to the assessor with photo "proof" that the interior wasn't done, so a 554 was filed. I don't believe anyone confirmed the validity of said proof. (and yes, in real life, we generally get the 554s from the assessors
lol).
In reading Opinion of Counsel 9-23, I agree that it's a gray area, and could justify it either way (I'd lean toward a denial--they haven't said a peep about the increase until now...after they're already a month late on their C/T bill that includes relevied
school...I'm much less inclined to be flexible at this point).
Kathleen Kearney, Director
Real Property Tax Services
Onondaga County
421 Montgomery St, 15th Floor
Syracuse, New York 13202
www.ongov.net/RPTS
P: (315) 435-2426
From: Real Property Tax Directors <RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US> on behalf of Daniel T. Martonis <0000001531d5a264-dmarc-request@LIST-NYSAC.US>
Sent: Wednesday, February 25, 2026 10:41 AM
To: RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US <RPTD@LIST-NYSAC.US>
Subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) What constitutes "error in essential fact"?
NOTICE: This email originated from
outside of Onondaga County's email system. Use caution with links and attachments.
You're dealing with a couple of different timelines with this "error."
If it's after tentative but before final, then the error should go on a 552. If it's lowering an assessment, they can use a 524 as well. In either case, these have to go in front of the BAR. You have no
say in it.
If it's after final, then it's either a 553, 554, or 556 depending on the timing. You have no say in the 553, but you have to do your research for the 554 and 556. If this "error" came in on one of those,
then it's up to you to give your recommendation as to if you agree, or disagree, with it. This is the only time that you have actual power. You can ask the assessor to give you everything they can about the correction, including the photos that they mention.
You can ask to see their files at the town hall. You can also ask the owner for the information (go around a contentious assessor if you wish). In truth, the assessor shouldn't even be in the chain of a correction unless you ask them to. In real life, we know
that the person is probably going to them first.
If their response, or actions, don't satisfy you, then recommend a denial. It's ultimately up to your legislature then.
For a blanket statement, I have recommended corrections due to percent complete as of taxable status day. I have also denied them due to lack of proof.
Daniel T. Martonis, CCD
Director of Real Property Tax Services
Chair, Cattaraugus County Land Bank
Board Chair, NYSACDRPTS
Cattaraugus County

I have an assessor who has, in the past, made assessment stipulations/changes after tentative roll (and even after final roll), so when we got a correction request to lower an AV from $1,020,700 to $400,000 because
"partial assessment increased as a completed property...per photos of inside given to assessor property is not completed inside" I was cautious to allow it without double checking. This is a big reduction and will mean going to our already contentious county
legislature asking them to approve a reduction of nearly $20,000 between the school and county/town taxes (which they hadn't paid). In the grand scheme of huge budgets, spread across 3 entities, it's not a lot, but with things sometimes getting heated in the
legislature, I want to be certain in what we send to them! In your opinions, is this an error in essential fact that we just approve, since the assessor signed off on it, or is it a "they should have gone to BAR/SCAR" situation?

External email detected. Do not click on links or open attachments from unknown sources. Be alert for phishing attempts & report suspicious email IT Security.
Good morning -
I have a follow-up question related to a question I had asked previously.
The backstory - A property owner had requested via a parcel combo form for my tax mapper to combine two adjacent parcels, and she denied it twice because the ownership was not the same.
On parcel A - The son is the sole owner. On parcel B - The son is the owner and the mother has Life Use.
Now the son filed a deed stating that the intention of the deed is to merge the two parcels.
So, my previous question was - Would you merge them? The lawyer is pushing the issue looking for tax law for why we can't.
At the time of my question, one of you (thank you) sent me this Op of Counsel
Volume 5 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 118
How I read that is that the assessor could make the determination whether to allow the parcels to be merged on the role, though this would be for assisting with assessing and tax bill purposes, and NOT in
determination of legal ownership. Ok... fine with that.
Now the lawyer states that the intention is also for the mother's Life Use to carry to the newly MERGED parcel, even though it states nothing about her extending Life Use in the deed to the newly merged parcel.
In fact, she is not mentioned in the deed and did not sign it.
On top of that, the parcel with the house is NOT currently the one the mother has Life Use on. Instead, the son lives there and has a Basic STAR on it. (The other parcel is a vacant lot.)
Would you put the Life Use on the new parcel? The only thing that the new deed states is that the FATHER's Life Use was extinguished because he passed away, but nothing about the mother's life use.
Even if it was put on, and if the mother is living there, too - and if she applied for an Enhanced STAR, it would have to be a credit, not an exemption. What a cluster.
I would appreciated any thoughts. This lawyer is being... persistent.
Thank you and Happy Halloween!!!
~ Meghan.

After things started getting back to normal after Covid, I continued to do my BAR training via Zoom for quite a few years. I shared the state's power point on my screen,
and I could see by the members cameras that they actually attended for the whole thing. That worked pretty well.
Last year was the first year that I went back to doing it in-person, and I am doing it that way this year. The zoom option may work best for some people.
I have occasionally had people that absolutely couldn't fit in my or any nearby trainings. I did have them watch the state's 3-hour video and sign a document confirming that
they watched it. Honestly, it would take less time out of their life to attend the training, as it seldom goes 3 hours.
Anyway, I only gave this option to members that have been on the BAR before. New members had to attend either my or another county's training.
I much prefer when they can attend a training, whether it is in-person or via Zoom because we get some good discussions going, and I can emphasis certain points.
Going to see how this year goes, and then decide whether to go back to the zoom training next year. Both have their advantages and disadvantages!
~ Meghan.

subject: tax bill apportionment
body:
Good afternoon -
I had an assessor ask me if it is too late to do an apportionment for the town & county tax bill. I've never had an apportionment done except during the first month of collection.
My understanding is that the assessor MAY (but is not required to approve an apportionment).
Do you have assessors that do apportionments this late into the town collection period? The tax collector would clearly have to calculate penalties on each of the new bills, as well.
On top of that, there is a school tax relevy on the bill (which would have to go on the original owner's portion).
How would you advise the assessor?
Thanks for any input. We only get a handful of apportionment requests here and they are usually when the tax bill first comes out.
~ Meghan.
Meghan K. Kincaid
Director for Real Property Tax Services
Yates County
417 Liberty Street, Suite 1093
Penn Yan, NY  14527

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) Demolition properties
body:
It's so much harder now. The only demos that we can now do are ones that have such a high starting figure that people won't bid. We start all our properties at
the back taxes owed. For the ones we want to demo, we make sure to put all the comments from the code enforcer on them. Even then, people are still buying them for stupid amounts.
Those that do make it through the first auction, we then do a second auction on location and in person at 8am on a Wednesday morning. That all about guarantees
that no one will show up. Then we give them to the land bank for nothing.

subject: Re: tax bill apportionment
body:
Yes it can be
apportioned and no, I don't believe it is optional.
Real Property
Tax
§  932. Payment
of taxes on part of a parcel of real property. 1.  The
collecting officer shall receive the tax on part of  a  parcel
of  real
property  provided  the  person offering to pay such
tax shall furnish a
particular specification of such part, including an apportionment
of the
assessment thereof made by the assessor after due notice to the
parties
affected. In the event that the tax on the remainder remains unpaid,
the
collecting  officer  shall enter such specification on
his return to the
county treasurer, indicating the part on which the tax  remains
unpaid.
If  the part on which the tax was paid is an undivided share,
the person
paying the same shall furnish the collecting officer with  the
name  of
the owner thereof, which shall be entered on the return of unpaid
taxes,
and  the  share  of such owner shall be excepted
in case of sale for the
tax on the remainder.
2. The county treasurer may, with respect to any taxes returned
to him
as unpaid, receive the taxes on part of a parcel of real property
in the
same manner  and  subject  to  the  same
conditions  as  set  forth  in
subdivision one of this section.
William E. Fuller,
CCD

Livingston County Government Center

Geneseo, NY 14454

Good
afternoon -
I
had an assessor ask me if it is too late to do an apportionment for the
town & county tax bill. I've never had an apportionment done except
during the first month of collection.
My
understanding is that the assessor MAY (but is not required to approve
an apportionment).
Do
you have assessors that do apportionments this late into the town collection
period? The tax collector would clearly have to calculate penalties on
each of the new bills, as well.
On
top of that, there is a school tax relevy on the bill (which would have
to go on the original owner's portion).
How
would you advise the assessor?
Thanks
for any input. We only get a handful of apportionment requests here and
they are usually when the tax bill first comes out.
~

subject: Re: tax bill apportionment
body:
As long as there is a tax to be collected, we will do a Certificate of Apportionment.
I will get notified by my Finance Office that the prior year's T/C taxes were not paid and now they see the parcel is subdivided.  They will request that I do a Cert of Apportionment so that
the newly subdivided parcels can get their share of the taxes that are over a year old.  The County can't put those unpaid taxes on 1.-1-1 as that doesn't exist anymore so I'll apportion to 1.-1-1.1 and 1.-1-1.2.  So as long as taxes are to be paid and they
need to be paid partially due to a split, I'll do a Cert of Apportionment.
And yes - not optional.
We also do
Memos of Apportionments.  This to assist in the closing for a split/subdivision so the attorneys can divide the taxes that have already been paid.  It doesn't appear that this service is done by other counties.  We will charge $30 to do this service.
Jay Franklin

Good afternoon -
I had an assessor ask me if it is too late to do an apportionment for the town & county tax bill. I've never had an apportionment done except during the first month of collection.
My understanding is that the assessor MAY (but is not required to approve an apportionment).
Do you have assessors that do apportionments this late into the town collection period? The tax collector would clearly have to calculate penalties on each of the new bills, as well.
On top of that, there is a school tax relevy on the bill (which would have to go on the original owner's portion).
How would you advise the assessor?
Thanks for any input. We only get a handful of apportionment requests here and they are usually when the tax bill first comes out.

subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] PILOT
body:
I'm no municipal attorney, but since PILOTs are a contract between the property owner and whatever entity that gave them that contract (usually an IDA), if the terms of the contract are broken, such as by non-payment, it is up to the IDA to take action, usually involving lots of lawyers. Often, it is spelled out in the PILOT agreement what will happen if they do not pay.
I believe that the IDA would have to cancel the PILOT and have it returned to the tax roll and then after that if they don't make tax payments, the County could eventually foreclose. But before that, it is all between the IDA and the property owner.
We have had just such a situation here in Orange County, where an adult home stopped making PILOT payments for the last five or so years of the PILOT. They were reportedly in such financial straits that the IDA did not want to end the PILOT and so we couldn't foreclose.

body:
Yes - see the form instructions (Form RP-41-A-INS:9/08:Instructions for Application for Property Tax Exemption for Industrial Development
Agencies:rp412ains). Property is entitled to the exemption if it's owned by, or under the jurisdiction or control, of the IDA. A PILOT isn't a prerequisite to the exemption, but the IDA does need to prove their interest in the property if they're not an
owner which would most commonly be the PILOT or something like a MOU.

subject: Re: Forestry Exemption
body:
Coleen,
The five-year plans should be filed with the DEC.  It is not up to the assessor to verify that the timber management plan is being followed.  If they do not file the plan accordingly, the DEC will notify them
of their failure to comply with the requirements of the Plan and give them a specific timeframe to report.  If they do not, they owner is subject to penalties, which the DEC will notify the treasurer's office and the property owner and a penalty chargeback
will be initiated.

Coleen,
The five-year plans should be filed with the DEC.  It is not up to the assessor to verify that the timber management plan is being followed.  If they do not file the plan accordingly, the DEC will notify them
of their failure to comply with the requirements of the Plan and give them a specific timeframe to report.  If they do not, they owner is subject to penalties, which the DEC will notify the treasurer's office and the property owner and a penalty chargeback

subject: Leased Land Under Solar Array - PILOT Question
body:
Hello all,  I could use some help on a correction application I received.
I've received an RP-554 from a property owner that leases about 14.5 acres to a solar developer.  The basis of the claim is that the PILOT calls for the developer to pay for the taxes on the "Project Facility"
which includes the land.  My first thought was absolutely not correctable because the land is not paid through the PILOT.  But when I read the PILOT, it indicates "Pursuant to the provisions of the Lease Agreement (which we are not privy to) the Company will
be required to pay all taxes and assessments lawfully levied and/or assessed against the Project Facility..."
The PILOT further indicates that the "Company" shall submit payment for the "Land" associated with the "Project Facility" to the receiver of taxes at 100% assessed value based on current tax rates, etc.
The landowner never requested the 14.5 acres be split from their 65 acres and the assessor has assessed the 14.5 acres as commercial.  The RP-554 and supporting letter from their attorney is proclaiming that
the property owner's taxes should only be based on the 50 +/- acres remaining after the leased land is deducted.
Any suggestions on this one?
Candy Akin, CCD
Real Property Tax Director
2025-2026 President, NYSACDRPTS
O: 315-376-5336
M: 315-907-2032
candyakin@lewiscounty.ny.gov
7660 North State St. | Lowville, NY 13367

subject: Solar/Wind Model
body:
I got a question on the model instructions. While computing the tax load, the instructions say:
"This required user input should be set equal to the overall full value tax rate for the property where the plant is sited. This rate should reflect
all property taxes applicable to the property, including town, county, village, school district, and special district tax rates."
My question is on the "...all property taxes applicable to the property..." Traditional IDA PILOTs do not include special district taxes. They get their own bill, fully taxable. Does this mean that the special district rate should not be used
because it is not "applicable" to the property? If you use it, then the assessment would go up. This would cause a double tax scenario. Tax on the model assessment and a tax bill on the special districts.
For those that do, what rates do you include while calculating the tax load?
I asked ORPTS but they were of no help. They just told me that the model is a draft right now...which has nothing to do with my question...

subject: Re: [External] Solar/Wind Model
body:
I do not use the tax rates when I'm determining my tax load.  I will put in the PILOT payment as the land lease payment.  And then add in a land value.
None of my solar projects have ever paid the full tax load - over 30 projects so far.  That is a fictitious assumption to use the full tax load.  You should use the 'taxes' that they are going to pay.  If a property doesn't have to pay
full taxes - the value of the property is higher.  We should recognize that.
I've been doing this since the calculator came out and the developers haven't said anything yet.

I got a question on the model instructions. While computing the tax load, the instructions say:
"This required user input should be set equal to the overall full value tax rate for the property where the plant is sited. This rate should reflect
all property taxes applicable to the property, including town, county, village, school district, and special district tax rates."
My question is on the "...all property taxes applicable to the property..." Traditional IDA PILOTs do not include special district taxes. They get their own bill, fully taxable. Does this mean that the special district rate should not be used
because it is not "applicable" to the property? If you use it, then the assessment would go up. This would cause a double tax scenario. Tax on the model assessment and a tax bill on the special districts.
For those that do, what rates do you include while calculating the tax load?
I asked ORPTS but they were of no help. They just told me that the model is a draft right now...which has nothing to do with my question...

body:

subject: veterans exemption - more changes??
body:
Good morning -
Our director of veterans' services was just in my office. He heard at a meeting yesterday that there is yet
another amendment proposed to the new 100% veterans disability exemption. The primary purpose of this amendment would be to
remove the requirement that the veteran must qualify for the "VA's specially adapted housing grant".
If this requirement is taken out, this mandatory exemption would have a huge impact, with pretty much all 100% disabled veteran homeowners qualifying for it.
Has anyone else heard anything about a proposed new amendment?
Thank you,
Meghan.
