NYS Real Property Tax Law §471
Surviving Spouse Exemption for Police Officers Killed in the Line of Duty
Overview
New York's Real Property Tax Law §471 provides a 50% property tax exemption for the primary residence of a surviving spouse of a police officer killed in the line of duty, if the local government or school district adopts the exemption by local law or resolution.
This summary consolidates the exact statutory text of RPTL §471 and the controlling definition of "surviving spouse" from EPTL §5‑1.2, which determines eligibility--including the effect of remarriage.
1. Exact Text: Real Property Tax Law §471
Source: NewYork.Public.Law
"§ 471 Surviving spouses of police officers killed in the line of duty
After the local legislative body of a county, city, town, or village passes a local law, or a school district passes a resolution, notwithstanding any other provision of law, real property owned by a surviving spouse of a police officer killed in the line of duty, and constituting the primary residence of such surviving spouse shall be exempt from taxation to the extent of fifty per centum of the assessed valuation thereof. Within such local law or resolution, the local legislative body or school district may reduce the percentage of exemption authorized pursuant to this section.
As used in this section, the term "police officer" shall have the same meaning as defined in section 1.20 of the criminal procedure law."
Important: §471 does not define "surviving spouse." New York law requires using the definition in the Estates, Powers & Trusts Law (EPTL) when a statute uses that term without defining it.
2. Exact Text: EPTL §5‑1.2 -- Disqualification as Surviving Spouse
Source: FindLaw (NY Consolidated Laws)
"§ 5‑1.2 Disqualification as surviving spouse (a) A husband or wife is a surviving spouse within the meaning, and for the purposes of 4‑1.1, 5‑1.1, 5‑1.1‑A, 5‑1.3, 5‑3.1 and 5‑4.4, unless it is established satisfactorily to the court having jurisdiction of the action or proceeding that:
(1) A final decree or judgment of divorce, of annulment or declaring the nullity of a marriage or dissolving such marriage on the ground of absence, recognized as valid under the law of this state, was in effect when the deceased spouse died.
(2) The marriage was void as incestuous under section five of the domestic relations law, bigamous under section six thereof, or a prohibited remarriage under section eight thereof.
3. How the Two Statutes Work Together
RPTL §471 grants the exemption only to a "surviving spouse of a police officer killed in the line of duty."
Because §471 does not define the term, the EPTL definition applies automatically.
Under New York law, a person is a "surviving spouse" only while they remain unmarried after the officer's death.
Remarriage ends eligibility, because the individual is no longer the surviving spouse of the deceased officer.
This rule is consistent across all NY survivor‑based exemptions (military, volunteer firefighter, etc.).
4. Practical Implications
Eligibility ends at the next taxable status date after remarriage.
Local assessors may require notification of any change in marital status.
The exemption applies only if adopted by the county, town, village, or school district.
5. Key Takeaway
The exemption under RPTL §471 applies only while the applicant remains the unremarried surviving spouse of the fallen police officer. Remarriage legally ends the status of "surviving spouse," and therefore ends the exemption.

Source: NewYork.Public.Law
"§ 471 Surviving spouses of police officers killed in the line of duty

real property owned by a surviving spouse of a police officer killed in the line of duty, and constituting the primary residence of such surviving spouse shall be exempt from taxation to the extent of fifty per centum of the assessed valuation thereof. Within
such local law or resolution, the local legislative body or school district may reduce the percentage of exemption authorized pursuant to this section.

state, was in effect when the deceased spouse died.

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) tax enforcement for separately assessed mobile homes
body:
We would threaten foreclosure on the whole park since it's just a courtesy split that's needed due to exemptions.
Is that the legal way? Not sure, but it has always worked.
We haven't had this issue in many years because what they now do is to have their people give them the tax bills (or get them online). The parks then pays all the taxes and divides it up for a monthly fee
added to their rent. The parks collect the taxes this way so they have no excuse for non-payment.

After things started getting back to normal after Covid, I continued to do my BAR training via Zoom for quite a few years. I shared the state's power point on my screen,
and I could see by the members cameras that they actually attended for the whole thing. That worked pretty well.
Last year was the first year that I went back to doing it in-person, and I am doing it that way this year. The zoom option may work best for some people.
I have occasionally had people that absolutely couldn't fit in my or any nearby trainings. I did have them watch the state's 3-hour video and sign a document confirming
that they watched it. Honestly, it would take less time out of their life to attend the training, as it seldom goes 3 hours.
Anyway, I only gave this option to members that have been on the BAR before. New members had to attend either my or another county's training.
I much prefer when they can attend a training, whether it is in-person or via Zoom because we get some good discussions going, and I can emphasis certain points.
Going to see how this year goes, and then decide whether to go back to the zoom training next year. Both have their advantages and disadvantages!
~ Meghan.

body:

Well, it is a courtesy split. You don't HAVE to do them. They are just a courtesy to the property owner. Tell them that you can delete all the courtesy splits then and merge all the exemptions onto one parcel

It sounds like the park in question makes their owners pay their taxes directly. None of mine do that.

Good morning -
I have a follow-up question related to a question I had asked previously.
The backstory - A property owner had requested via a parcel combo form for my tax mapper to combine two adjacent parcels, and she denied it twice because the ownership was not the same.
On parcel A - The son is the sole owner. On parcel B - The son is the owner and the mother has Life Use.
Now the son filed a deed stating that the intention of the deed is to merge the two parcels.
So, my previous question was - Would you merge them? The lawyer is pushing the issue looking for tax law for why we can't.
At the time of my question, one of you (thank you) sent me this Op of Counsel
Volume
5 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 118
How I read that is that the assessor could make the determination whether to allow the parcels to be merged on the role, though this would be for assisting with assessing and tax bill purposes, and NOT in
determination of legal ownership. Ok... fine with that.
Now the lawyer states that the intention is also for the mother's Life Use to carry to the newly MERGED parcel, even though it states nothing about her extending Life Use in the deed to the newly merged parcel.
In fact, she is not mentioned in the deed and did not sign it.
On top of that, the parcel with the house is NOT currently the one the mother has Life Use on. Instead, the son lives there and has a Basic STAR on it. (The other parcel is a vacant lot.)
Would you put the Life Use on the new parcel? The only thing that the new deed states is that the FATHER's Life Use was extinguished because he passed away, but nothing about the mother's life use.
Even if it was put on, and if the mother is living there, too - and if she applied for an Enhanced STAR, it would have to be a credit, not an exemption. What a cluster.
I would appreciated any thoughts. This lawyer is being... persistent.
Thank you and Happy Halloween!!!
~ Meghan.

AFTER the bill has been paid or the collection period has expired--but then what does CREDIT mean on that form?  When would there ever be a 'credit' if it weren't before the bill was paid, and it was figured out, and you correct the bill by 'crediting' the
amount owed by the mistake?

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) One more Correction question
body:
I don't mess with the "credit" word in the 556. I think Jay had a good definition once, but I forgot it. I
think it has to do with those that accept partial payments, but I'm not sure. We don't.
I stick to what I said for my stuff.
The 556 law about it only says:
"10. When a portion of an outstanding tax has been credited pursuant to
this  section, any interest and penalties that have been imposed thereon
shall be reduced to the extent that such  interest  and  penalties  were
attributable  to  the  credited  portion  of  the tax, and no additional
interest and penalties shall be imposed if the corrected amount  of  the
tax  is  paid  within  eight  days  of  the  date on which the notice of
approval is mailed pursuant to paragraph (e) of subdivision five of this
section."

Subject: merging parcels
Caution: This is an external email. Please take care when clicking links or opening attachments. When in doubt, contact the Help Desk.
Good morning -
I have a follow-up question related to a question I had asked previously.
The backstory - A property owner had requested via a parcel combo form for my tax mapper to combine two adjacent parcels, and she denied it twice because the ownership was not the same.
On parcel A - The son is the sole owner. On parcel B - The son is the owner and the mother has Life Use.
Now the son filed a deed stating that the intention of the deed is to merge the two parcels.
So, my previous question was - Would you merge them? The lawyer is pushing the issue looking for tax law for why we can't.
At the time of my question, one of you (thank you) sent me this Op of Counsel Volume 5 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 118
How I read that is that the assessor could make the determination whether to allow the parcels to be merged on the role, though this would be for assisting with assessing and tax bill purposes, and NOT in determination of legal ownership. Ok... fine with that.
Now the lawyer states that the intention is also for the mother's Life Use to carry to the newly MERGED parcel, even though it states nothing about her extending Life Use in the deed to the newly merged parcel. In fact, she is not mentioned in the deed and did not sign it.
On top of that, the parcel with the house is NOT currently the one the mother has Life Use on. Instead, the son lives there and has a Basic STAR on it. (The other parcel is a vacant lot.)
Would you put the Life Use on the new parcel? The only thing that the new deed states is that the FATHER's Life Use was extinguished because he passed away, but nothing about the mother's life use.
Even if it was put on, and if the mother is living there, too - and if she applied for an Enhanced STAR, it would have to be a credit, not an exemption. What a cluster.
I would appreciated any thoughts. This lawyer is being... persistent.
Thank you and Happy Halloween!!!
~ Meghan.

subject: 48660 Housing Development Fund CTS
body:
Happy Friday afternoon all -
I have a parcel with a 48660 exemption in roll section 1.  Years ago, heard reference to 577-c regarding this parcel.  The owners/developer was able to make a 'benefit agreement' to pay only the village a small amount each year in lieu
of taxes.  The school and town were not part of that conversation.  The property was recently purchased through foreclosure.  The village has reached out to see if taxes for the village, school and town could be charged, back to when the new company took ownership.
The new owners have not filed for the exemption to my knowledge.  What are the laws regarding this?  I appreciate your help as always and hope to see you at the conference.
Thank you,
Tiffany

subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) One more Correction question
body:
The "credit" in terms of RP 556 means crediting the amount being collected by the County Treasurer. If the Warrant has expired it's now with the Treasurer: if they paid the tax they
get a refund, if they didn't pay it the Treasurer credits the balance.
cred·​it
\ˈkre-dit\
n : a deduction from an amount otherwise due

Subject: Re: (EXTERNAL) One more Correction question
I don't mess with the "credit" word in the 556. I think Jay had a good definition once, but I forgot it. I
think it has to do with those that accept partial payments, but I'm not sure. We don't.
I stick to what I said for my stuff.
The 556 law about it only says:
"10. When a portion of an outstanding tax has been credited pursuant to
this  section, any interest and penalties that have been imposed thereon
shall be reduced to the extent that such  interest  and  penalties  were
attributable  to  the  credited  portion  of  the tax, and no additional
interest and penalties shall be imposed if the corrected amount  of  the
tax  is  paid  within  eight  days  of  the  date on which the notice of
approval is mailed pursuant to paragraph (e) of subdivision five of this
section."

Caution: This is an external email. Please take care when clicking links or opening attachments. When in doubt, contact the Help Desk.
Good morning -
I have a follow-up question related to a question I had asked previously.
The backstory - A property owner had requested via a parcel combo form for my tax mapper to combine two adjacent parcels, and she denied it twice because the ownership was not the same.
On parcel A - The son is the sole owner. On parcel B - The son is the owner and the mother has Life Use.
Now the son filed a deed stating that the intention of the deed is to merge the two parcels.
So, my previous question was - Would you merge them? The lawyer is pushing the issue looking for tax law for why we can't.
At the time of my question, one of you (thank you) sent me this Op of Counsel
Volume 5 - Opinions of Counsel SBEA No. 118
How I read that is that the assessor could make the determination whether to allow the parcels to be merged on the role, though this would be for assisting with assessing and tax bill purposes, and NOT in
determination of legal ownership. Ok... fine with that.
Now the lawyer states that the intention is also for the mother's Life Use to carry to the newly MERGED parcel, even though it states nothing about her extending Life Use in the deed to the newly merged parcel.
In fact, she is not mentioned in the deed and did not sign it.
On top of that, the parcel with the house is NOT currently the one the mother has Life Use on. Instead, the son lives there and has a Basic STAR on it. (The other parcel is a vacant lot.)
Would you put the Life Use on the new parcel? The only thing that the new deed states is that the FATHER's Life Use was extinguished because he passed away, but nothing about the mother's life use.
Even if it was put on, and if the mother is living there, too - and if she applied for an Enhanced STAR, it would have to be a credit, not an exemption. What a cluster.
I would appreciated any thoughts. This lawyer is being... persistent.
Thank you and Happy Halloween!!!
~ Meghan.

Learn why this is important
Good morning everyone,
I want to add my "thank you" to Corey here for advice, laws and links! Thank you, Corey!
Also, in Jefferson County we establish a "Last Day Village Collectors can collect" each year.  I believe in the past they have generally used the last business day in October for this and the extension has been considered a courtesy to Village Collectors
and property owners.

Unpaid water/sewer: Town law 198 covers a lot of topics but Water (3(d)
NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov) specifically says that no later than November 1st the town clerk must file with the Supervisor a list of unpaid water accounts and
the supervisor shall then transmit such statements to "the board of supervisors of the county at its next regular meeting"
Alternatively what I do: just make your life easy and say everything needs to be submitted at the same time the Town budget is submitted to the County. Towns have until November
20th to pass a budget (NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov), the Town Clerk must deliver within 5 day the final budget to the Town Supervisor (NYS
Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov), and the Town Supervisor must send the budget to the County within 10 days of receiving it from the Clerk (NYS Open Legislation | NYSenate.gov).
So - at the end of the day, December 5th is the absolute latest a town can submit their budget to the County and the budget should include the amounts to be raised for any relevies to be added to tax bills.
